# Genetic and Epigenetic Landscapes of Bladder Cancer and Implications for Early Detection and Precision Medicine

Bladder cancer (BCa), especially urothelial carcinoma, is defined by pronounced molecular heterogeneity spanning mutations, copy-number alterations, and epigenomic reprogramming that together drive initiation, progression, recurrence, and therapy resistance. <cite id="c632b87b-0">Advancements in genomic and molecular research have provided unprecedented insights into the intricate pathways and genetic and epigenetic alterations driving bladder cancer tumorigenesis, progression, and therapeutic resistance</cite> <cite id="c632b87b-1">Comprehensive genomic and transcriptomic analyses have identified distinct molecular subtypes, mutations, copy-number alterations, and epigenetic modifications in bladder cancer, enabling refined patient stratification for precision medicine and improving early detection via methylation markers and SNP sites</cite> <cite id="c632b87b-2">Epigenomic control proteins and unique genetic alterations underpin BCa heterogeneity; integrating genomic and molecular profiling into diagnostics can facilitate early detection, guide therapy, and monitor progression</cite>. Below, we synthesize core landscape features and translate them into actionable strategies for early detection and precision oncology.

## Genetic Landscape: Drivers, Copy-Number Instability, and Molecular Subtypes

Genome-wide programs such as TCGA and large-scale consortia consistently identify recurrent alterations concentrated in pathways controlling cell cycle, chromatin, and receptor tyrosine kinase signaling, with notable co-occurrence and mutual exclusivity patterns that demarcate clinically relevant subtypes. <cite id="d5c38272-0">Analyses of bladder cancer specimens revealed 302 mutations across exons, alterations within 204 copy-number segments, and 20 genomic rearrangements; recurrent mutations include TP53, FGFR3, PIK3CA, MLL2, CDKN1A, and ERGC2; TP53 alterations occur in approximately half of cases and are associated with genomic instability and prognosis, while FGFR3 alterations are frequent in non-invasive disease and drop in muscle-invasive tumors</cite>. <cite id="d5c38272-2">Across 4,631 tumors in the GENIE database, frequent mutations include TP53, TERT, KDM6A, KMT2D, ARID1A, and FGFR3, with co-occurrence patterns (e.g., TP53 with RB1) and mutual exclusivity (e.g., TP53 with FGFR3 or KDM6A) defining molecular subtypes</cite>.

These alterations co-localize with extensive structural variation and tumor-ecosystem remodeling. <cite id="d5c38272-0">Alterations within 204 copy-number segments and 20 rearrangements were observed, reflecting high genomic burden in bladder cancer akin to lung and melanoma</cite> <cite id="d5c38272-1">Integrating mutations, fusions, and copy number data across cohorts shows FGFR3 genomic alterations are enriched in LumP tumors (55%, p<0.001), with additional class-specific features such as KDM6A and CDKN2A deletion patterns</cite>. Cell-line reference maps further cluster tumors by driver pathways and genomic instability. <cite id="d5c38272-4">Genomic profiling of 40 UBC cell lines reveals mutation patterns and copy-number alterations consistent with FGFR3-driven and TP53/RB1-driven tumor pathways, with focal gains/losses, frequent UPD, and X chromosome losses suggesting tumor suppressor loci; aggressive subtypes predominate among available lines</cite>.

Early-stage (nonmuscle-invasive, NMIBC) disease also exhibits substantial genomic heterogeneity that correlates with risk and progression. <cite id="d5c38272-3">A comprehensive genomic analysis of 800 NMIBC tumors found large genomic variation with frequent FGFR3 loss of heterozygosity and 17p (TP53) loss in tumors with respective mutations; 15% harbor whole-genome doubling associated with worse outcomes, genomic instability in cell-cycle genes, and altered immune composition; integrative multi-omics highlights genomic instability and immune exhaustion linked to progression</cite>. Transcriptomic subtyping complements these signals. <cite id="053ed7f1-3">Lund expression subtypes categorize tumors into Urobasal A (frequent FGFR3 mutations, favorable prognosis), Urobasal B (progressed Urobasal A), Genomically Unstable (high grade, instability), squamous cell carcinoma-like (poor prognosis, basal markers), and infiltrated classes, providing clinically relevant categories tied to targeted therapy</cite>.

## Epigenetic Landscape: Chromatin Remodeling, DNA Methylation, and Enhancer Dynamics

Beyond DNA mutations, bladder cancer is characterized by pervasive epigenetic reprogramming that controls lineage gene expression, promotes plasticity, and shapes immune evasion and therapy response. <cite id="053ed7f1-0">In urothelial cancer, mutations in chromatin-modifying genes are among the most common alterations, affecting histone methyltransferases and demethylases; subtype-specific ChIP-seq mapping of H3K27me3 and H3K4 methylation marks reveals epigenetic differences across muscle-invasive subtypes</cite>. <cite id="053ed7f1-1">Epigenetic dysregulation of chromatin remodeling, histone modification, and DNA methylation is pivotal in initiation, progression, and resistance; ARID1A, KMT2C/KMT2D, EP300, CREBBP, and EZH2 mutations disrupt nucleosome positioning and enhancer function, sculpting intratumoral heterogeneity, transcriptional plasticity, and immune escape, and thereby impacting responses to chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and targeted therapy</cite>.

DNA methylation patterns stratify disease and link to prognosis and therapeutic vulnerabilities. <cite id="053ed7f1-2">DNA methylation plays an important role in initiation and progression of bladder cancer; integrative high-throughput analyses from TCGA demonstrate diverse genetic and epigenetic alterations, and DNA methylation is reversible, supporting development of epigenetic therapies</cite>. <cite id="053ed7f1-3">Gene expression and epigenomic interrelations define UC subtypes; few studies have interrogated the epigenomic landscape of UC, underscoring the need for integrated genome–methylation–expression mapping to prioritize causal epigenetic events</cite>. Functionally, enhancer and promoter methylation, together with histone marks, distinguish molecular subtypes and may underpin differential dependency on epigenetic regulators. <cite id="053ed7f1-0">Mapping H3K27me3 and H3K4 mono/tri-methylation in primary bladder tumors demarcates enhancer/promoter states across basal/squamous, luminal, and neuroendocrine-like subtypes, providing an epigenetic basis for subtype-specific behaviors</cite>.

## From Landscape to Early Detection: Biomarkers and Diagnostic Platforms

Molecular heterogeneity yields multiple tractable biomarkers for early detection, spanning tissue and urine-based assays that capture mutations, methylation, and expression features, with validation showing high tissue–urine congruence and actionable signal enrichment.

- Tissue-based profiling and methylation markers: <cite id="c632b87b-1">Molecular subtyping using NGS and methylation markers enables early detection and targeted therapeutic monitoring, with integration into diagnostic protocols improving accuracy and stratification</cite> <cite id="d5c38272-0">High mutational burden in bladder cancer provides rich targets for screening and diagnosis; TP53 and FGFR3 alterations are prevalent and prognostic, supporting use as salient biomarkers</cite>.
- Urine and cfDNA/ctDNA: <cite id="d5c38272-0">Urine is accessible and shows high concordance with tissue DNA, enabling noninvasive screening, diagnosis, and longitudinal assessment; numerous studies report strong congruence between urine and tumor DNA</cite>. <cite id="053ed7f1-1">Epigenetic biomarkers based on mutation profiles, chromatin accessibility, and DNA methylation signatures offer non-invasive strategies for early detection, disease monitoring, and patient stratification in urine or plasma</cite>.
- Subtype-specific early detection: <cite id="d5c38272-1">Consensus molecular classes show class-specific alterations such as FGFR3 enrichment in LumP tumors and CDKN2A deletion patterns; such profiles provide a blueprint for subtype-tailored detection and risk models</cite>. <cite id="d5c38272-3">In NMIBC, genomic instability and immune exhaustion signatures are linked to aggressiveness, suggesting utility of instability-related methylation and immune markers for early risk stratification</cite>.
- Practical performance considerations: <cite id="d5c38272-0">Urine-based assays avoid invasive biopsy and show high congruence with tissue, supporting longitudinal monitoring; FGFR3 and TP53 can guide targeted surveillance</cite>. <cite id="c632b87b-4">Methylation markers and SNP sites in combination with NGS and bioinformatics pipelines can yield precise diagnostic tools to enhance early detection and timely interventions</cite>.

Collectively, these data support multi-omic, minimally invasive diagnostic cascades: urine DNA/methylation screens for early-stage detection with reflex tissue confirmation and targeted genomic profiling to subtype risk and nominate targeted or immunotherapy strategies. <cite id="c632b87b-0">Integration of methylation markers and SNP sites into diagnostic accuracy is poised to become a cornerstone of bladder cancer management, improving early detection and precision treatment</cite> <cite id="053ed7f1-1">Urine/plasma-based epigenetic biomarkers enable non-invasive early detection, monitoring, and stratification; epigenetic alterations provide mechanistic, biomarker, and therapeutic implications</cite>.

## Precision Medicine: Molecular Subtypes, Targeted Therapies, and Immunotherapy

Molecular classification provides the substrate for precision selection of systemic and local therapies, with distinct genomic and epigenomic dependencies that can be targeted.

- FGFR-driven disease: <cite id="d5c38272-1">LumP tumors are enriched for FGFR3 mutations (~33–40% when adding targeted FGFR sequencing), with frequent KDM6A alterations; these tumors often harbor CDKN2A deletions, supporting FGFR/HRD-sensitive strategies</cite>. <cite id="d5c38272-0">FGFR3 alterations are strongly associated with non-invasive disease and decline in muscle-invasive cases, aligning with a paradigm where FGFR-pathway inhibition is pivotal in NMIBC and selected MIBC settings</cite>.
- PI3K/AKT/mTOR and Ras-pathway alterations: <cite id="d5c38272-0">PIK3CA mutations are recurrent and participate in key cell-cycle pathways; together with RAS alterations, they form actionable nodes for targeted agents, particularly in genomically unstable or luminal subtypes</cite> <cite id="d5c38272-3">Genomically unstable tumors with whole-genome doubling and cell-cycle gene alterations point to PI3K/AKT/mTOR and MAPK pathway activation as rational targets for synthetic lethality or targeted kinase inhibition</cite>.
- Chromatin/EZH2/DNMT/HDAC/BET targeting and immune evasion: <cite id="053ed7f1-1">Mutations in ARID1A, KMT2C/D, EP300, CREBBP, and EZH2 drive enhancer dysfunction and transcriptional plasticity that facilitate immune evasion; epigenetic biomarkers in urine or plasma are actionable for stratification, and EZH2, HDAC, BET, DNMT, and chromatin remodeling inhibitors—alone or in combinations with ICIs, chemotherapy, or targeted agents—are under active investigation</cite>. <cite id="053ed7f1-0">Histone methylation mark profiling connects subtype identity to epigenetic vulnerabilities that can be probed pharmacologically</cite>.
- Immunotherapy biomarkers: <cite id="c632b87b-4">Tumors with heightened immune activation correlate with superior 5-year disease-specific survival in bladder cancer, suggesting immune-hot subtypes may derive benefit from immunotherapy</cite>. <cite id="053ed7f1-1">Epigenetic remodeling can modulate immunogenicity and immune microenvironment; biomarker strategies that integrate chromatin and DNA methylation signatures with tumor mutational burden and PD-L1 status can refine selection for checkpoint inhibitors</cite>.
- Patient stratification and risk-adapted care: <cite id="d5c38272-3">In NMIBC, WGD, cell-cycle alterations, and immune exhaustion associate with progression, enabling genomic and immune-based risk models that guide escalated therapy, surveillance intensity, or bladder-sparing strategies</cite> <cite id="053ed7f1-3">Urobasal A (FGFR3-mutant) has a good prognosis, whereas Genomically Unstable and SCC-like tumors are high grade/high risk, supporting tailored management</cite>. <cite id="d5c38272-2">Mutational patterns and co-mutational patterns (e.g., TP53 with RB1 vs TP53 with FGFR3/KDM6A) define clinically distinct entities, motivating molecularly guided clinical trial assignment and targeted agent development</cite>.

Taken together, precision medicine in bladder cancer is moving from one-size-fits-all chemotherapy to subtype- and mechanism-informed regimens that combine targeted agents to address driver alterations and epigenetic dependencies, immune-oncology strategies tuned to tumor-immune contextures, and epigenetic modulators to sensitize tumors and immune microenvironments. <cite id="053ed7f1-1">Translational strategies include non-invasive epigenetic biomarkers for early detection and monitoring, and therapeutic classes targeting EZH2, HDAC, BET, DNMT, and chromatin remodelers, often in combination with ICIs or targeted therapies</cite> <cite id="c632b87b-0">Integration of genetic and epigenetic markers into diagnostic-therapeutic pathways promises to improve patient outcomes and quality of life through personalized treatment strategies</cite>.

## Clinical Implementation: From Evidence to Practice

Implementing these insights requires diagnostic pathways that capture both germline-to-somatic alterations and reversible epigenetic lesions, with parallel clinical workflows for surveillance and therapy selection.

- Diagnostic algorithms: <cite id="d5c38272-0">Urine-based mutation and methylation assays can screen for early-stage disease and track genomic evolution noninvasively, with tissue biopsy reserved for definitive molecular profiling and therapeutic decision-making</cite> <cite id="c632b87b-1">Methylation markers and SNP sites integrated with NGS enable early detection and therapeutic monitoring, enhancing diagnostic accuracy and precision care</cite>.
- Risk-adapted treatment: <cite id="d5c38272-3">NMIBC patients with WGD and genomic instability should be risk-stratified for early muscle-invasive progression and immune exhaustion, prompting consideration of more aggressive intravesical or surgical strategies and immune modulation</cite> <cite id="d5c38272-1">FGFR3-mutant LumP tumors are candidates for FGFR-pathway inhibitors and HRD-exploiting combinations, while SCC-like/basal-like tumors merit PI3K/AKT/mTOR, MAPK, and immune-based regimens</cite>.
- Overcoming resistance: <cite id="053ed7f1-1">Epigenetic plasticity driven by chromatin modifier mutations fosters resistance; combining DNA-demethylating agents, EZH2 inhibitors, and BET/HDAC inhibitors with targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitors or checkpoint blockade may restore sensitivity</cite>.
- Biomarker development: <cite id="053ed7f1-0">ChIP-seq maps of histone methylation marks in primary tumors provide a resource to discover subtype-specific enhancer vulnerabilities and to design epigenetic biomarker panels for early detection and therapy selection</cite>.

## Challenges and Future Directions

Key challenges include standardizing multi-omic assays in community settings, reconciling sampling variability in urine biomarkers, and delineating minimal-residual disease eradication endpoints for biomarker-driven de-escalation strategies. <cite id="d5c38272-0">Urine assays show high tissue congruence, but optimization of capture and sequencing panels is needed for robust sensitivity and specificity in early detection</cite>. <cite id="053ed7f1-1">Integrating mechanistic epigenetic data with clinical endpoints will be essential to validate non-invasive biomarkers for stratification and monitoring</cite>. Emerging technologies and AI-driven integration are poised to close gaps. <cite id="053ed7f1-1">Single-cell and spatial genomics combined with AI-facilitated multi-omics integration enable high-resolution maps of tumor heterogeneity, enhancer dynamics, and epigenetic vulnerabilities, accelerating translational biomarker discovery</cite>. Longitudinal studies and prospective trials are needed to calibrate early detection strategies to actionable endpoints and to benchmark targeted regimens by molecular subtype.

In summary, convergent genetic and epigenetic evidence defines bladder cancer as a heterogeneous disease with reproducible, clinically informative subtypes and reversible epigenetic lesions that can be targeted for early detection and precision therapy. <cite id="d5c38272-2">Frequent mutations in TP53, TERT, KDM6A, KMT2D, ARID1A, and FGFR3, with characteristic co-occurrence/mutual exclusivity patterns, underpin molecular stratification</cite> <cite id="053ed7f1-1">Chromatin and DNA methylation alterations drive transcriptional plasticity and immune evasion, creating therapeutic vulnerabilities accessible via non-invasive biomarkers</cite>. Clinically, this translates into urine-first screening with reflex tissue molecular profiling for subtype-specific risk models, targeted systemic therapies (FGFR-pathway inhibitors for FGFR3-driven disease; PI3K/mTOR or MAPK inhibitors for PIK3CA/RAS alterations), epigenetic modulators to sensitize tumors and immune microenvironments, and immunotherapy tailored to immune-activated phenotypes, with AI-assisted multi-omics to refine selection and monitor response. <cite id="c632b87b-0">By integrating methylation markers and SNP sites into diagnostics, early detection and precision therapeutic pathways can be deployed to improve patient outcomes and the management of urothelial bladder carcinoma</cite>.

Title: Epigenetic profiling demarcates molecular subtypes of muscle-invasive bladder cancer
Snippet: The luminal subtypes express markers of terminal urothelial differentiation, such as uroplakins. The basal/ squamous and neuroendocrine-like subtypes show distinct expression signatures 12 . The understanding of the underlying biological mechanisms defining the molecular bladder cancer subtypes has yet to develop. Using gene expression data to find upstream regulators of the molecular subtypes, Choi et al. found that luminal MIBC exhibit peroxisome proliferator activator receptor (PPAR) pathway activation and high expression levels of PPARG 10 . Also, Eriksson et al. showed that molecular subtypes differ in the expression of urothelial differentiation programs involving PPARG/RXRA, FOXA1, GATA3, and anterior HOXA and HOXB genes 17 . 

Interestingly, of all TCGA cancer types, mutations in chromatin-modifying genes were most common in urothelial cancer and encompassed histone methyltransferases and demethylases 5 . However, the extent and localization of chromatin modifications in primary bladder tumours as well as their functional consequences, remain uncharted territory. To better understand the epigenetics of bladder cancer subtypes, we assessed multiple histone methylation marks in chemotherapy-naïve primary urothelial cancer samples. We used chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP-seq) to pinpoint genomic regions with histone methylation marks in subgroups of patients. We mapped histone 3-lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3), a marker for repressed genes, and histone 3-lysine 4-mono-and tri-methylation, which are indicators of active enhancers and active promoters respectively. Here we provide a detailed overview of three histone methylation marks that gives insight into the epigenetic differences between MIBC subtypes. Also, this unique data-set of genome-wide ChIP-seq data of histone methylation marks in primary bladder tumours will serve as a valuable new resource for the bladder cancer community.
</snippet>

Title: Epigenetic Alterations and Chromatin Landscape Remodeling in Urothelial Bladder Cancer: Molecular Drivers, Biomarker Potential, and Emerging Therapeutic Strategies
Snippet: Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder (UBC) is a heterogeneous disease from the clinicopathologic and molecular standpoint and presents clinical management problems for its range in progression, frequent recurrence and complicated genetic/epigenetic architecture. These changes sculpt the tumor microenvironment and impact the response to chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and targeted therapy.Epigenetic biomarkers based on mutation profiles, chromatin accessibility and DNA methylation signatures present new non-invasive strategies that can be followed for early detection, monitoring of disease and stratification of patients usage; which are all available in urine or plasma. Title: Integrative analysis of the epigenetic basis of muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma
Snippet: Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder is the eighth most common form of cancer in the USA and the fourth most common type of cancer in men [1]. Although the majority of urothelial carcinoma of the bladder is diagnosed at a non-invasive stage, 30-40% of cases will progress to invade the deeper muscle layer of the bladder [2], at which point the long-term disease-specific survival is 50-70% [3,4]. 

Multiple studies have shown that DNA methylation, the process by which a methyl group is added to a cytosine residue of a cytosine-phosphate-guanine (CpG) dinucleotide, plays an important role in the initiation and progression of bladder cancer [5][6][7]. DNA methylation represents a promising target for therapy since DNA methylation is a reversible process that does not alter the content of DNA [8]. 

High-throughput methods have been employed in bladder cancer to evaluate the epigenetic alterations involved in the development and progression of this disease [5,9]. However, many methylation events found to be statistically significant using high-throughput screening methods are not correlated with gene expression changes [10]. There is a need for high-throughput approaches that integrate data across multiple platforms to determine the epigenetic events that are most likely to be involved in bladder cancer [11]. 

The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) project demonstrated impressive diversity in both genetic and epigenetic alterations within patients who have muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma of the bladder [12]. The multiple platforms utilized within TCGA make it possible to perform analyses integrating data from multiple sources to identify specific abnormalities most likely to contribute to oncogenic processes. In this study, we utilized an integrative approach to evaluate the epigenetic processes that may be most important in development and progression of invasive urothelial carcinoma.
</snippet>
<snippet id=053ed7f1-3>
Title: Integrative epigenomic analysis of differential DNA methylation in urothelial carcinoma
Snippet: Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder (UC) is one of the most common epithelial malignancies in the industrialized world and is characterized by heterogeneity in terms of the underlying molecular mechanisms. With respect to histopathology, UC can broadly be subdivided into non-muscle-invasive (NMI, stages Ta and T1) and muscle-invasive (MI, stage ≥ T2) disease. NMI disease is generally associated with a good prognosis despite frequent recurrences while MI disease has a decidedly worse prognosis [1]. Pioneering studies on phenotypic characterization of tumors using gene expression profiling have provided valuable insight into tumor biology and allowed for clinically relevant patient stratification with respect to targeted therapies [2,3]. We have previously established a molecular classification system for UC based on global gene expression patterns (Lund subtypes), and defined five major biologically distinct classes of tumors [4]. The Lund gene expression subtypes of UC include: (1) the low stage and grade Urobasal A tumors characterized by frequent FGFR3 mutations and a good prognosis; (2) high stage and grade Urobasal B tumors that are likely progressed Urobasal A tumors; (3) Genomically Unstable tumors characterized by high tumor grade and genomic instability; (4) the poor prognosis squamous cell carcinoma-like (SCC-like) tumors characterized by expression of basal cell markers; and (5) Infiltrated tumors in which the intrinsic gene expression subtype is partially confounded by infiltrating immune and stromal cells [4,5]. 

Alterations in DNA methylation and chromatin modification patterns are linked features that underlie many of the phenotypic changes observed in cancer cells [6]. In recent years, the interrelations between the gene expression phenotype, the genome, as well as the DNA methylation landscape has been extensively investigated across different malignancies [7,8]. Few studies have investigated the epigenomic landscape of UC.
</snippet>

Title: Analysis of urine cell-free DNA in bladder cancer diagnosis by emerging bioactive technologies and materials
Snippet: Mutations and accumulations within proto-oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes in somatic cells are critical hallmarks of malignant tumors. Like lung cancer and melanoma, bladder cancer exhibits high mutation rate, emerging as a malignancy with a significant mutational burden. Analyses of bladder cancer specimens revealed 302 mutations across exons, alterations within 204 copy number segments at the genomic level, and 20 instances of genomic rearrangements (Cancer Genome Atlas Research, 2014). Recent research has identified mutations in genes such as TP53, FGFR3, PIK3CA, MLL2, CDKN1A, and ERGC2 in patients with bladder cancer. These genetic aberrations play pivotal roles in essential physiological mechanisms, including cell cycle control and programmed cell death. Notably, alterations in the tumor suppressor gene TP53 are detectable in approximately half of the cases (Cancer Genome Atlas Research, 2014). As a critical driver gene in bladder cancer, TP53 inactivation disrupts normal cellular cycle checkpoints, fostering genomic instability that promotes tumorigenesis. Additionally, TP53 expression levels correlate with bladder cancer progression and serve as significant prognostic indicators (Hollstein et al., 1991). Alterations in FGFR3 also constitute critical mutations in bladder cancer, displaying strong associations with disease stage and grade; approximately 78.1% of patients with non-invasive bladder cancer showed FGFR3 expression, whereas the expression rate dropped to 18.2% in muscle-invasive cases (Akanksha and Sandhya, 2019). Thus, mutational profiles are salient biomarkers for bladder cancer, promising tools for tumor screening, diagnosis, and ongoing assessment to elucidate tumorigenic pathways. 

Obtaining tumor mutational data from tissue biopsies provides insights into cancer progression but is hindered by its invasive nature, which poses risks of complications and limits its use for longterm monitoring. Urine, readily accessible with minimal protein contamination and directly interacting with bladder cancer cells, is a preferable alternative. Numerous studies corroborate the high concordance between urine and tissue samples in terms of tumor DNA congruence (Ou et al., 2020;Zhang et al., 2021;Hirotsu et al., 2019).
</snippet>

Title: Genomic Characteristics of Bladder Cancer: An AACR Project GENIE Study
Snippet: Bladder and urothelial carcinoma are marked by profound genomic diversity. Using a large, multi-institutional dataset, we performed comprehensive genomic profiling of 4631 tumor samples from 4050 individuals. A retrospective analysis of bladder and urothelial cancer was performed using the AACR Project GENIE database. Demographic associations, mutation frequencies, copy number changes, and survival correlations were analyzed with a p-value < 0.05. Frequent mutations were identified in TP53, TERT, KDM6A, KMT2D, ARID1A, and FGFR3. Mutation frequencies varied by sex and race, with specific alterations enriched in female and Asian patients. Distinct patterns of co-occurrence, including TP53 with RB1, and mutual exclusivity, including TP53 with FGFR3 or KDM6A, revealed distinct molecular subtypes. This study highlights the extensive heterogeneity of bladder cancer, and our findings emphasize the clinical importance of molecular stratification and support the need for further mechanistic and prospective studies to inform the development of targeted therapies.
</snippet>

Title: Comprehensive genomic characterization of early-stage bladder cancer
Snippet: Understanding the molecular landscape of nonmuscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) is essential to improve risk assessment and treatment regimens. We performed a comprehensive genomic analysis of patients with NMIBC using whole-exome sequencing (n = 438), shallow whole-genome sequencing (n = 362) and total RNA sequencing (n = 414). A large genomic variation within NMIBC was observed and correlated with different molecular subtypes. Frequent loss of heterozygosity in FGFR3 and 17p (affecting TP53) was found in tumors with mutations in FGFR3 and TP53, respectively. Whole-genome doubling (WGD) was observed in 15% of the tumors and was associated with worse outcomes. Tumors with WGD were genomically unstable, with alterations in cell-cycle-related genes and an altered immune composition. Finally, integrative clustering of multi-omics data highlighted the important role of genomic instability and immune cell exhaustion in disease aggressiveness. These findings advance our understanding of genomic differences associated with disease aggressiveness in NMIBC and may ultimately improve patient stratification. A genomic and transcriptomic analysis of nonmuscle-invasive bladder cancer identifies four molecular subtypes, and associates whole-genome duplication and immune exhaustion with tumor progression.
</snippet>

Title: The UBC-40 Urothelial Bladder Cancer cell line index: a genomic resource for functional studies
Snippet: Urothelial bladder cancer is a highly heterogeneous disease. Cancer cell lines are useful tools for its study. This is a comprehensive genomic characterization of 40 urothelial bladder carcinoma (UBC) cell lines including information on origin, mutation status of genes implicated in bladder cancer (FGFR3, PIK3CA, TP53, and RAS), copy number alterations assessed using high density SNP arrays, uniparental disomy (UPD) events, and gene expression. Based on gene mutation patterns and genomic changes we identify lines representative of the FGFR3-driven tumor pathway and of the TP53/RB tumor suppressor-driven pathway. High-density array copy number analysis identified significant focal gains (1q32, 5p13.1-12, 7q11, and 7q33) and losses (i.e. 6p22.1) in regions altered in tumors but not previously described as affected in bladder cell lines. We also identify new evidence for frequent regions of UPD, often coinciding with regions reported to be lost in tumors. Previously undescribed chromosome X losses found in UBC lines also point to potential tumor suppressor genes. Cell lines representative of the FGFR3-driven pathway showed a lower number of UPD events. Overall, there is a predominance of more aggressive tumor subtypes among the cell lines. We provide a cell line classification that establishes their relatedness to the major molecularly-defined bladder tumor subtypes. The compiled information should serve as a useful reference to the bladder cancer research community and should help to select cell lines appropriate for the functional analysis of bladder cancer genes, for example those being identified through massive parallel sequencing.

# Genetic and Epigenetic Landscapes of Bladder Cancer and Implications for Early Detection and Precision Medicine

Bladder cancer (BCa), especially urothelial carcinoma, is defined by pronounced molecular heterogeneity spanning mutations, copy-number alterations, and epigenomic reprogramming that together drive initiation, progression, recurrence, and therapy resistance. <cite id="c632b87b-0">Advancements in genomic and molecular research have provided unprecedented insights into the intricate pathways and genetic and epigenetic alterations driving bladder cancer tumorigenesis, progression, and therapeutic resistance</cite> <cite id="c632b87b-1">Comprehensive genomic and transcriptomic analyses have identified distinct molecular subtypes, mutations, copy-number alterations, and epigenetic modifications in bladder cancer, enabling refined patient stratification for precision medicine and improving early detection via methylation markers and SNP sites</cite> <cite id="c632b87b-2">Epigenomic control proteins and unique genetic alterations underpin BCa heterogeneity; integrating genomic and molecular profiling into diagnostics can facilitate early detection, guide therapy, and monitor progression</cite>. Below, we synthesize core landscape features and translate them into actionable strategies for early detection and precision oncology.

## Genetic Landscape: Drivers, Copy-Number Instability, and Molecular Subtypes

Genome-wide programs such as TCGA and large-scale consortia consistently identify recurrent alterations concentrated in pathways controlling cell cycle, chromatin, and receptor tyrosine kinase signaling, with notable co-occurrence and mutual exclusivity patterns that demarcate clinically relevant subtypes. <cite id="d5c38272-0">Analyses of bladder cancer specimens revealed 302 mutations across exons, alterations within 204 copy-number segments, and 20 genomic rearrangements; recurrent mutations include TP53, FGFR3, PIK3CA, MLL2, CDKN1A, and ERGC2; TP53 alterations occur in approximately half of cases and are associated with genomic instability and prognosis, while FGFR3 alterations are frequent in non-invasive disease and drop in muscle-invasive tumors</cite>. <cite id="d5c38272-2">Across 4,631 tumors in the GENIE database, frequent mutations include TP53, TERT, KDM6A, KMT2D, ARID1A, and FGFR3, with co-occurrence patterns (e.g., TP53 with RB1) and mutual exclusivity (e.g., TP53 with FGFR3 or KDM6A) defining molecular subtypes</cite>.

These alterations co-localize with extensive structural variation and tumor-ecosystem remodeling. <cite id="d5c38272-0">Alterations within 204 copy-number segments and 20 rearrangements were observed, reflecting high genomic burden in bladder cancer akin to lung and melanoma</cite> <cite id="d5c38272-1">Integrating mutations, fusions, and copy number data across cohorts shows FGFR3 genomic alterations are enriched in LumP tumors (55%, p<0.001), with additional class-specific features such as KDM6A and CDKN2A deletion patterns</cite>. Cell-line reference maps further cluster tumors by driver pathways and genomic instability. <cite id="d5c38272-4">Genomic profiling of 40 UBC cell lines reveals mutation patterns and copy-number alterations consistent with FGFR3-driven and TP53/RB1-driven tumor pathways, with focal gains/losses, frequent UPD, and X chromosome losses suggesting tumor suppressor loci; aggressive subtypes predominate among available lines</cite>.

Early-stage (nonmuscle-invasive, NMIBC) disease also exhibits substantial genomic heterogeneity that correlates with risk and progression. <cite id="d5c38272-3">A comprehensive genomic analysis of 800 NMIBC tumors found large genomic variation with frequent FGFR3 loss of heterozygosity and 17p (TP53) loss in tumors with respective mutations; 15% harbor whole-genome doubling associated with worse outcomes, genomic instability in cell-cycle genes, and altered immune composition; integrative multi-omics highlights genomic instability and immune exhaustion linked to progression</cite>. Transcriptomic subtyping complements these signals. <cite id="053ed7f1-3">Lund expression subtypes categorize tumors into Urobasal A (frequent FGFR3 mutations, favorable prognosis), Urobasal B (progressed Urobasal A), Genomically Unstable (high grade, instability), squamous cell carcinoma-like (poor prognosis, basal markers), and infiltrated classes, providing clinically relevant categories tied to targeted therapy</cite>.

## Epigenetic Landscape: Chromatin Remodeling, DNA Methylation, and Enhancer Dynamics

Beyond DNA mutations, bladder cancer is characterized by pervasive epigenetic reprogramming that controls lineage gene expression, promotes plasticity, and shapes immune evasion and therapy response. <cite id="053ed7f1-0">In urothelial cancer, mutations in chromatin-modifying genes are among the most common alterations, affecting histone methyltransferases and demethylases; subtype-specific ChIP-seq mapping of H3K27me3 and H3K4 methylation marks reveals epigenetic differences across muscle-invasive subtypes</cite>. <cite id="053ed7f1-1">Epigenetic dysregulation of chromatin remodeling, histone modification, and DNA methylation is pivotal in initiation, progression, and resistance; ARID1A, KMT2C/KMT2D, EP300, CREBBP, and EZH2 mutations disrupt nucleosome positioning and enhancer function, sculpting intratumoral heterogeneity, transcriptional plasticity, and immune escape, and thereby impacting responses to chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and targeted therapy</cite>.

DNA methylation patterns stratify disease and link to prognosis and therapeutic vulnerabilities. <cite id="053ed7f1-2">DNA methylation plays an important role in initiation and progression of bladder cancer; integrative high-throughput analyses from TCGA demonstrate diverse genetic and epigenetic alterations, and DNA methylation is reversible, supporting development of epigenetic therapies</cite>. <cite id="053ed7f1-3">Gene expression and epigenomic interrelations define UC subtypes; few studies have interrogated the epigenomic landscape of UC, underscoring the need for integrated genome–methylation–expression mapping to prioritize causal epigenetic events</cite>. Functionally, enhancer and promoter methylation, together with histone marks, distinguish molecular subtypes and may underpin differential dependency on epigenetic regulators. <cite id="053ed7f1-0">Mapping H3K27me3 and H3K4 mono/tri-methylation in primary bladder tumors demarcates enhancer/promoter states across basal/squamous, luminal, and neuroendocrine-like subtypes, providing an epigenetic basis for subtype-specific behaviors</cite>.

## From Landscape to Early Detection: Biomarkers and Diagnostic Platforms

Molecular heterogeneity yields multiple tractable biomarkers for early detection, spanning tissue and urine-based assays that capture mutations, methylation, and expression features, with validation showing high tissue–urine congruence and actionable signal enrichment.

- Tissue-based profiling and methylation markers: <cite id="c632b87b-1">Molecular subtyping using NGS and methylation markers enables early detection and targeted therapeutic monitoring, with integration into diagnostic protocols improving accuracy and stratification</cite> <cite id="d5c38272-0">High mutational burden in bladder cancer provides rich targets for screening and diagnosis; TP53 and FGFR3 alterations are prevalent and prognostic, supporting use as salient biomarkers</cite>.
- Urine and cfDNA/ctDNA: <cite id="d5c38272-0">Urine is accessible and shows high concordance with tissue DNA, enabling noninvasive screening, diagnosis, and longitudinal assessment; numerous studies report strong congruence between urine and tumor DNA</cite>. <cite id="053ed7f1-1">Epigenetic biomarkers based on mutation profiles, chromatin accessibility, and DNA methylation signatures offer non-invasive strategies for early detection, disease monitoring, and patient stratification in urine or plasma</cite>.
- Subtype-specific early detection: <cite id="d5c38272-1">Consensus molecular classes show class-specific alterations such as FGFR3 enrichment in LumP tumors and CDKN2A deletion patterns; such profiles provide a blueprint for subtype-tailored detection and risk models</cite>. <cite id="d5c38272-3">In NMIBC, genomic instability and immune exhaustion signatures are linked to aggressiveness, suggesting utility of instability-related methylation and immune markers for early risk stratification</cite>.
- Practical performance considerations: <cite id="d5c38272-0">Urine-based assays avoid invasive biopsy and show high congruence with tissue, supporting longitudinal monitoring; FGFR3 and TP53 can guide targeted surveillance</cite>. <cite id="c632b87b-4">Methylation markers and SNP sites in combination with NGS and bioinformatics pipelines can yield precise diagnostic tools to enhance early detection and timely interventions</cite>.

Collectively, these data support multi-omic, minimally invasive diagnostic cascades: urine DNA/methylation screens for early-stage detection with reflex tissue confirmation and targeted genomic profiling to subtype risk and nominate targeted or immunotherapy strategies. <cite id="c632b87b-0">Integration of methylation markers and SNP sites into diagnostic accuracy is poised to become a cornerstone of bladder cancer management, improving early detection and precision treatment</cite> <cite id="053ed7f1-1">Urine/plasma-based epigenetic biomarkers enable non-invasive early detection, monitoring, and stratification; epigenetic alterations provide mechanistic, biomarker, and therapeutic implications</cite>.

## Precision Medicine: Molecular Subtypes, Targeted Therapies, and Immunotherapy

Molecular classification provides the substrate for precision selection of systemic and local therapies, with distinct genomic and epigenomic dependencies that can be targeted.

- FGFR-driven disease: <cite id="d5c38272-1">LumP tumors are enriched for FGFR3 mutations (~33–40% when adding targeted FGFR sequencing), with frequent KDM6A alterations; these tumors often harbor CDKN2A deletions, supporting FGFR/HRD-sensitive strategies</cite>. <cite id="d5c38272-0">FGFR3 alterations are strongly associated with non-invasive disease and decline in muscle-invasive cases, aligning with a paradigm where FGFR-pathway inhibition is pivotal in NMIBC and selected MIBC settings</cite>.
- PI3K/AKT/mTOR and Ras-pathway alterations: <cite id="d5c38272-0">PIK3CA mutations are recurrent and participate in key cell-cycle pathways; together with RAS alterations, they form actionable nodes for targeted agents, particularly in genomically unstable or luminal subtypes</cite> <cite id="d5c38272-3">Genomically unstable tumors with whole-genome doubling and cell-cycle gene alterations point to PI3K/AKT/mTOR and MAPK pathway activation as rational targets for synthetic lethality or targeted kinase inhibition</cite>.
- Chromatin/EZH2/DNMT/HDAC/BET targeting and immune evasion: <cite id="053ed7f1-1">Mutations in ARID1A, KMT2C/D, EP300, CREBBP, and EZH2 drive enhancer dysfunction and transcriptional plasticity that facilitate immune evasion; epigenetic biomarkers in urine or plasma are actionable for stratification, and EZH2, HDAC, BET, DNMT, and chromatin remodeling inhibitors—alone or in combinations with ICIs, chemotherapy, or targeted agents—are under active investigation</cite>. <cite id="053ed7f1-0">Histone methylation mark profiling connects subtype identity to epigenetic vulnerabilities that can be probed pharmacologically</cite>.
- Immunotherapy biomarkers: <cite id="c632b87b-4">Tumors with heightened immune activation correlate with superior 5-year disease-specific survival in bladder cancer, suggesting immune-hot subtypes may derive benefit from immunotherapy</cite>. <cite id="053ed7f1-1">Epigenetic remodeling can modulate immunogenicity and immune microenvironment; biomarker strategies that integrate chromatin and DNA methylation signatures with tumor mutational burden and PD-L1 status can refine selection for checkpoint inhibitors</cite>.
- Patient stratification and risk-adapted care: <cite id="d5c38272-3">In NMIBC, WGD, cell-cycle alterations, and immune exhaustion associate with progression, enabling genomic and immune-based risk models that guide escalated therapy, surveillance intensity, or bladder-sparing strategies</cite> <cite id="053ed7f1-3">Urobasal A (FGFR3-mutant) has a good prognosis, whereas Genomically Unstable and SCC-like tumors are high grade/high risk, supporting tailored management</cite>. <cite id="d5c38272-2">Mutational patterns and co-mutational patterns (e.g., TP53 with RB1 vs TP53 with FGFR3/KDM6A) define clinically distinct entities, motivating molecularly guided clinical trial assignment and targeted agent development</cite>.

Taken together, precision medicine in bladder cancer is moving from one-size-fits-all chemotherapy to subtype- and mechanism-informed regimens that combine targeted agents to address driver alterations and epigenetic dependencies, immune-oncology strategies tuned to tumor-immune contextures, and epigenetic modulators to sensitize tumors and immune microenvironments. <cite id="053ed7f1-1">Translational strategies include non-invasive epigenetic biomarkers for early detection and monitoring, and therapeutic classes targeting EZH2, HDAC, BET, DNMT, and chromatin remodelers, often in combination with ICIs or targeted therapies</cite> <cite id="c632b87b-0">Integration of genetic and epigenetic markers into diagnostic-therapeutic pathways promises to improve patient outcomes and quality of life through personalized treatment strategies</cite>.

## Clinical Implementation: From Evidence to Practice

Implementing these insights requires diagnostic pathways that capture both germline-to-somatic alterations and reversible epigenetic lesions, with parallel clinical workflows for surveillance and therapy selection.

- Diagnostic algorithms: <cite id="d5c38272-0">Urine-based mutation and methylation assays can screen for early-stage disease and track genomic evolution noninvasively, with tissue biopsy reserved for definitive molecular profiling and therapeutic decision-making</cite> <cite id="c632b87b-1">Methylation markers and SNP sites integrated with NGS enable early detection and therapeutic monitoring, enhancing diagnostic accuracy and precision care</cite>.
- Risk-adapted treatment: <cite id="d5c38272-3">NMIBC patients with WGD and genomic instability should be risk-stratified for early muscle-invasive progression and immune exhaustion, prompting consideration of more aggressive intravesical or surgical strategies and immune modulation</cite> <cite id="d5c38272-1">FGFR3-mutant LumP tumors are candidates for FGFR-pathway inhibitors and HRD-exploiting combinations, while SCC-like/basal-like tumors merit PI3K/AKT/mTOR, MAPK, and immune-based regimens</cite>.
- Overcoming resistance: <cite id="053ed7f1-1">Epigenetic plasticity driven by chromatin modifier mutations fosters resistance; combining DNA-demethylating agents, EZH2 inhibitors, and BET/HDAC inhibitors with targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitors or checkpoint blockade may restore sensitivity</cite>.
- Biomarker development: <cite id="053ed7f1-0">ChIP-seq maps of histone methylation marks in primary tumors provide a resource to discover subtype-specific enhancer vulnerabilities and to design epigenetic biomarker panels for early detection and therapy selection</cite>.

## Challenges and Future Directions

Key challenges include standardizing multi-omic assays in community settings, reconciling sampling variability in urine biomarkers, and delineating minimal-residual disease eradication endpoints for biomarker-driven de-escalation strategies. <cite id="d5c38272-0">Urine assays show high tissue congruence, but optimization of capture and sequencing panels is needed for robust sensitivity and specificity in early detection</cite>. <cite id="053ed7f1-1">Integrating mechanistic epigenetic data with clinical endpoints will be essential to validate non-invasive biomarkers for stratification and monitoring</cite>. Emerging technologies and AI-driven integration are poised to close gaps. <cite id="053ed7f1-1">Single-cell and spatial genomics combined with AI-facilitated multi-omics integration enable high-resolution maps of tumor heterogeneity, enhancer dynamics, and epigenetic vulnerabilities, accelerating translational biomarker discovery</cite>. Longitudinal studies and prospective trials are needed to calibrate early detection strategies to actionable endpoints and to benchmark targeted regimens by molecular subtype.

In summary, convergent genetic and epigenetic evidence defines bladder cancer as a heterogeneous disease with reproducible, clinically informative subtypes and reversible epigenetic lesions that can be targeted for early detection and precision therapy. <cite id="d5c38272-2">Frequent mutations in TP53, TERT, KDM6A, KMT2D, ARID1A, and FGFR3, with characteristic co-occurrence/mutual exclusivity patterns, underpin molecular stratification</cite> <cite id="053ed7f1-1">Chromatin and DNA methylation alterations drive transcriptional plasticity and immune evasion, creating therapeutic vulnerabilities accessible via non-invasive biomarkers</cite>. Clinically, this translates into urine-first screening with reflex tissue molecular profiling for subtype-specific risk models, targeted systemic therapies (FGFR-pathway inhibitors for FGFR3-driven disease; PI3K/mTOR or MAPK inhibitors for PIK3CA/RAS alterations), epigenetic modulators to sensitize tumors and immune microenvironments, and immunotherapy tailored to immune-activated phenotypes, with AI-assisted multi-omics to refine selection and monitor response. <cite id="c632b87b-0">By integrating methylation markers and SNP sites into diagnostics, early detection and precision therapeutic pathways can be deployed to improve patient outcomes and the management of urothelial bladder carcinoma</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Advancing Genomics in Urologic Tumors: Navigating Precision Therapeutic Pathways
Snippet: Urologic cancers, with bladder cancer as a pivotal subtype, pose substantial challenges to global health, necessitating a profound understanding of their molecular underpinnings. This article explores recent genomic research, with a focus on transitional cell carcinoma, the primary histological form of transitional cell carcinoma, aiming to elucidate the intricate molecular processes that underlie the onset and advancement of disease. Title: Epigenetic profiling demarcates molecular subtypes of muscle-invasive bladder cancer
Snippet: The luminal subtypes express markers of terminal urothelial differentiation, such as uroplakins. The basal/ squamous and neuroendocrine-like subtypes show distinct expression signatures 12 . The understanding of the underlying biological mechanisms defining the molecular bladder cancer subtypes has yet to develop. Using gene expression data to find upstream regulators of the molecular subtypes, Choi et al. found that luminal MIBC exhibit peroxisome proliferator activator receptor (PPAR) pathway activation and high expression levels of PPARG 10 . Also, Eriksson et al. showed that molecular subtypes differ in the expression of urothelial differentiation programs involving PPARG/RXRA, FOXA1, GATA3, and anterior HOXA and HOXB genes 17 . 

Interestingly, of all TCGA cancer types, mutations in chromatin-modifying genes were most common in urothelial cancer and encompassed histone methyltransferases and demethylases 5 . However, the extent and localization of chromatin modifications in primary bladder tumours as well as their functional consequences, remain uncharted territory. To better understand the epigenetics of bladder cancer subtypes, we assessed multiple histone methylation marks in chemotherapy-naïve primary urothelial cancer samples. We used chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP-seq) to pinpoint genomic regions with histone methylation marks in subgroups of patients. We mapped histone 3-lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3), a marker for repressed genes, and histone 3-lysine 4-mono-and tri-methylation, which are indicators of active enhancers and active promoters respectively. Here we provide a detailed overview of three histone methylation marks that gives insight into the epigenetic differences between MIBC subtypes. Also, this unique data-set of genome-wide ChIP-seq data of histone methylation marks in primary bladder tumours will serve as a valuable new resource for the bladder cancer community.

Title: Epigenetic Alterations and Chromatin Landscape Remodeling in Urothelial Bladder Cancer: Molecular Drivers, Biomarker Potential, and Emerging Therapeutic Strategies
Snippet: Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder (UBC) is a heterogeneous disease from the clinicopathologic and molecular standpoint and presents clinical management problems for its range in progression, frequent recurrence and complicated genetic/epigenetic architecture. Not only traditional genetic changes, but also epigenetic dysregulation (e.g., alterations of chromatin remodeling, histone modification and DNA methylation) has been increasingly recognized to play a pivotal role in the process of tumor initiation, progression, metastasis and resistance to therapy. It is a dissapointing result that mutations of the chromatin remodeler such as ARID1A, KMT2C, KMT2D, and histone modifying enzymes (EP300, CREBBP and EZH2) not only cause loss-of-nucleosome positioning in addition lead to lack of enhancer function and perturbation ofT program contributing to shaping up intratumoral heterogeneity as well as transcriptional plasticity resulting in failure in immunoevasion. These changes sculpt the tumor microenvironment and impact the response to chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and targeted therapy.Epigenetic biomarkers based on mutation profiles, chromatin accessibility and DNA methylation signatures present new non-invasive strategies that can be followed for early detection, monitoring of disease and stratification of patients usage; which are all available in urine or plasma. Therapeutically, inhibitors of EZH2, HDACs, BET proteins, DNMTs and certain chromatin remodeling factors are currently being heavily investigated in preclinical studies or clinical trials as monotherapies or rational combinations with ICIs, chemotherapy or targeted therapies.Advances in tech nologies, such as single- and spatial genomics combined with AI-facilitated multi-omics integration make it possible to realize high-resolution maps of tumor heterogeneity, enhancer d namics, and epigenetic vulnerabilities. This review aims to present the current data on UBC epigenetic modifications and their mechanistic, biomarker and therapeutic implications. By combining mechanistic understanding with translational perspectives, we outline future directions

Title: Integrative analysis of the epigenetic basis of muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma
Snippet: Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder is the eighth most common form of cancer in the USA and the fourth most common type of cancer in men [1]. Although the majority of urothelial carcinoma of the bladder is diagnosed at a non-invasive stage, 30-40% of cases will progress to invade the deeper muscle layer of the bladder [2], at which point the long-term disease-specific survival is 50-70% [3,4]. 

Multiple studies have shown that DNA methylation, the process by which a methyl group is added to a cytosine residue of a cytosine-phosphate-guanine (CpG) dinucleotide, plays an important role in the initiation and progression of bladder cancer [5][6][7]. DNA methylation represents a promising target for therapy since DNA methylation is a reversible process that does not alter the content of DNA [8]. 

High-throughput methods have been employed in bladder cancer to evaluate the epigenetic alterations involved in the development and progression of this disease [5,9]. However, many methylation events found to be statistically significant using high-throughput screening methods are not correlated with gene expression changes [10]. There is a need for high-throughput approaches that integrate data across multiple platforms to determine the epigenetic events that are most likely to be involved in bladder cancer [11]. 

The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) project demonstrated impressive diversity in both genetic and epigenetic alterations within patients who have muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma of the bladder [12]. The multiple platforms utilized within TCGA make it possible to perform analyses integrating data from multiple sources to identify specific abnormalities most likely to contribute to oncogenic processes. In this study, we utilized an integrative approach to evaluate the epigenetic processes that may be most important in development and progression of invasive urothelial carcinoma.

Title: Integrative epigenomic analysis of differential DNA methylation in urothelial carcinoma
Snippet: Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder (UC) is one of the most common epithelial malignancies in the industrialized world and is characterized by heterogeneity in terms of the underlying molecular mechanisms. With respect to histopathology, UC can broadly be subdivided into non-muscle-invasive (NMI, stages Ta and T1) and muscle-invasive (MI, stage ≥ T2) disease. NMI disease is generally associated with a good prognosis despite frequent recurrences while MI disease has a decidedly worse prognosis [1]. Pioneering studies on phenotypic characterization of tumors using gene expression profiling have provided valuable insight into tumor biology and allowed for clinically relevant patient stratification with respect to targeted therapies [2,3]. We have previously established a molecular classification system for UC based on global gene expression patterns (Lund subtypes), and defined five major biologically distinct classes of tumors [4]. The Lund gene expression subtypes of UC include: (1) the low stage and grade Urobasal A tumors characterized by frequent FGFR3 mutations and a good prognosis; (2) high stage and grade Urobasal B tumors that are likely progressed Urobasal A tumors; (3) Genomically Unstable tumors characterized by high tumor grade and genomic instability; (4) the poor prognosis squamous cell carcinoma-like (SCC-like) tumors characterized by expression of basal cell markers; and (5) Infiltrated tumors in which the intrinsic gene expression subtype is partially confounded by infiltrating immune and stromal cells [4,5]. 

Alterations in DNA methylation and chromatin modification patterns are linked features that underlie many of the phenotypic changes observed in cancer cells [6]. In recent years, the interrelations between the gene expression phenotype, the genome, as well as the DNA methylation landscape has been extensively investigated across different malignancies [7,8]. Few studies have investigated the epigenomic landscape of UC.

Title: Advancing Genomics in Urologic Tumors: Navigating Precision Therapeutic Pathways
Snippet: The exploration of bladder cancer's molecular subtypes and understanding their experimental significance is important for tailoring treatment strategies and optimizing patient outcomes [23].A retrospective analysis revealed that tumors with heightened immune activation correlated with superior 5-year diseasespecific survival rates, suggesting a potential avenue for further research.The study dives into the molecular intricacies of earlystage urothelial bladder cancer and advanced urothelial bladder cancer, identifying distinct molecular subtypes with specific genetic characteristics [24].This highlights the necessity for detailed molecular profiling to decipher the disease's complex genetic landscape and underscores the potential for personalized therapeutic interventions tailored to individual patients' genetic profiles [25].

The integration of molecular subtyping and genomic profiling into diagnostic and treatment protocols holds significant promise for enhancing the management of bladder cancer.This groundbreaking study aims to revolutionize bladder cancer diagnostics by harnessing the potential of methylation markers and single nucleotide polymorphism sites [26].Leveraging cuttingedge next-generation sequencing technologies, sophisticated bioinformatics algorithms, and rigorous validation protocols, the study meticulously identifies potential diagnostic biomarkers associated with urothelial bladder carcinoma.The development of this precise diagnostic tool holds immense promise in enhancing early detection rates, facilitating timely interventions, and ultimately improving patient outcomes [27] .

By delving into the cellular landscape of urothelial cancer and harnessing the power of genomic profiling, this study seeks to pave the way for the development of a highly accurate and targeted diagnostic tool.The utilization of methylation markers and SNP sites, in combination with advanced NGS technologies and bioinformatics algorithms, aims to identify specific biomarkers that can aid in the early and precise detection of UBC [28].The successful development and implementation of this diagnostic tool have the potential to transform the clinical management of UBC, offering healthcare professionals a sophisticated and reliable method for detecting and diagnosing this complex malignancy [29].Ultimately, this innovation has the capacity to significantly improve patient outcomes by enabling timely interventions and tailored treatment strategies.The etiological landscape of bladder cancer is multifaceted, shaped by a complex interplay of genetic predispositions, environmental exposures, and lifestyle factors.

documents.snippet:
The luminal subtypes express markers of terminal urothelial differentiation, such as uroplakins. The basal/ squamous and neuroendocrine-like subtypes show distinct expression signatures 12 . The understanding of the underlying biological mechanisms defining the molecular bladder cancer subtypes has yet to develop. Using gene expression data to find upstream regulators of the molecular subtypes, Choi et al. found that luminal MIBC exhibit peroxisome proliferator activator receptor (PPAR) pathway activation and high expression levels of PPARG 10 . Also, Eriksson et al. showed that molecular subtypes differ in the expression of urothelial differentiation programs involving PPARG/RXRA, FOXA1, GATA3, and anterior HOXA and HOXB genes 17 . 

Interestingly, of all TCGA cancer types, mutations in chromatin-modifying genes were most common in urothelial cancer and encompassed histone methyltransferases and demethylases 5 . However, the extent and localization of chromatin modifications in primary bladder tumours as well as their functional consequences, remain uncharted territory. To better understand the epigenetics of bladder cancer subtypes, we assessed multiple histone methylation marks in chemotherapy-naïve primary urothelial cancer samples. We used chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP-seq) to pinpoint genomic regions with histone methylation marks in subgroups of patients. We mapped histone 3-lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3), a marker for repressed genes, and histone 3-lysine 4-mono-and tri-methylation, which are indicators of active enhancers and active promoters respectively. Here we provide a detailed overview of three histone methylation marks that gives insight into the epigenetic differences between MIBC subtypes. Also, this unique data-set of genome-wide ChIP-seq data of histone methylation marks in primary bladder tumours will serve as a valuable new resource for the bladder cancer community.

documents.title: Epigenetic Alterations and Chromatin Landscape Remodeling in Urothelial Bladder Cancer: Molecular Drivers, Biomarker Potential, and Emerging Therapeutic Strategies
documents.snippet: Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder (UBC) is a heterogeneous disease from the clinicopathologic and molecular standpoint and presents clinical management problems for its range in progression, frequent recurrence and complicated genetic/epigenetic architecture. Not only traditional genetic changes, but also epigenetic dysregulation (e.g., alterations of chromatin remodeling, histone modification and DNA methylation) has been increasingly recognized to play a pivotal role in the process of tumor initiation, progression, metastasis and resistance to therapy. It is a dissapointing result that mutations of the chromatin remodeler such as ARID1A, KMT2C, KMT2D, and histone modifying enzymes (EP300, CREBBP and EZH2) not only cause loss-of-nucleosome positioning in addition lead to lack of enhancer function and perturbation ofT program contributing to shaping up intratumoral heterogeneity as well as transcriptional plasticity resulting in failure in immunoevasion. These changes sculpt the tumor microenvironment and impact the response to chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and targeted therapy.Epigenetic biomarkers based on mutation profiles, chromatin accessibility and DNA methylation signatures present new non-invasive strategies that can be followed for early detection, monitoring of disease and stratification of patients usage; which are all available in urine or plasma. Therapeutically, inhibitors of EZH2, HDACs, BET proteins, DNMTs and certain chromatin remodeling factors are currently being heavily investigated in preclinical studies or clinical trials as monotherapies or rational combinations with ICIs, chemotherapy or targeted therapies.Advances in tech nologies, such as single- and spatial genomics combined with AI-facilitated multi-omics integration make it possible to realize high-resolution maps of tumor heterogeneity, enhancer d namics, and epigenetic vulnerabilities. This review aims to present the current data on UBC epigenetic modifications and their mechanistic, biomarker and therapeutic implications. By combining mechanistic understanding with translational perspectives, we outline future directions

documents.title: Integrative analysis of the epigenetic basis of muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma
documents.snippet:
Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder is the eighth most common form of cancer in the USA and the fourth most common type of cancer in men [1]. Although the majority of urothelial carcinoma of the bladder is diagnosed at a non-invasive stage, 30-40% of cases will progress to invade the deeper muscle layer of the bladder [2], at which point the long-term disease-specific survival is 50-70% [3,4]. 

Multiple studies have shown that DNA methylation, the process by which a methyl group is added to a cytosine residue of a cytosine-phosphate-guanine (CpG) dinucleotide, plays an important role in the initiation and progression of bladder cancer [5][6][7]. DNA methylation represents a promising target for therapy since DNA methylation is a reversible process that does not alter the content of DNA [8]. 

High-throughput methods have been employed in bladder cancer to evaluate the epigenetic alterations involved in the development and progression of this disease [5,9]. However, many methylation events found to be statistically significant using high-throughput screening methods are not correlated with gene expression changes [10]. There is a need for high-throughput approaches that integrate data across multiple platforms to determine the epigenetic events that are most likely to be involved in bladder cancer [11]. 

The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) project demonstrated impressive diversity in both genetic and epigenetic alterations within patients who have muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma of the bladder [12]. The multiple platforms utilized within TCGA make it possible to perform analyses integrating data from multiple sources to identify specific abnormalities most likely to contribute to oncogenic processes. In this study, we utilized an integrative approach to evaluate the epigenetic processes that may be most important in development and progression of invasive urothelial carcinoma.

documents.title: Integrative epigenomic analysis of differential DNA methylation in urothelial carcinoma
documents.snippet:
Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder (UC) is one of the most common epithelial malignancies in the industrialized world and is characterized by heterogeneity in terms of the underlying molecular mechanisms. With respect to histopathology, UC can broadly be subdivided into non-muscle-invasive (NMI, stages Ta and T1) and muscle-invasive (MI, stage ≥ T2) disease. NMI disease is generally associated with a good prognosis despite frequent recurrences while MI disease has a decidedly worse prognosis [1]. Pioneering studies on phenotypic characterization of tumors using gene expression profiling have provided valuable insight into tumor biology and allowed for clinically relevant patient stratification with respect to targeted therapies [2,3]. We have previously established a molecular classification system for UC based on global gene expression patterns (Lund subtypes), and defined five major biologically distinct classes of tumors [4]. The Lund gene expression subtypes of UC include: (1) the low stage and grade Urobasal A tumors characterized by frequent FGFR3 mutations and a good prognosis; (2) high stage and grade Urobasal B tumors that are likely progressed Urobasal A tumors; (3) Genomically Unstable tumors characterized by high tumor grade and genomic instability; (4) the poor prognosis squamous cell carcinoma-like (SCC-like) tumors characterized by expression of basal cell markers; and (5) Infiltrated tumors in which the intrinsic gene expression subtype is partially confounded by infiltrating immune and stromal cells [4,5]. 

Alterations in DNA methylation and chromatin modification patterns are linked features that underlie many of the phenotypic changes observed in cancer cells [6]. In recent years, the interrelations between the gene expression phenotype, the genome, as well as the DNA methylation landscape has been extensively investigated across different malignancies [7,8]. Few studies have investigated the epigenomic landscape of UC.

The exploration of bladder cancer's molecular subtypes and understanding their experimental significance is important for tailoring treatment strategies and optimizing patient outcomes [23].A retrospective analysis revealed that tumors with heightened immune activation correlated with superior 5-year diseasespecific survival rates, suggesting a potential avenue for further research.The study dives into the molecular intricacies of earlystage urothelial bladder cancer and advanced urothelial bladder cancer, identifying distinct molecular subtypes with specific genetic characteristics [24].This highlights the necessity for detailed molecular profiling to decipher the disease's complex genetic landscape and underscores the potential for personalized therapeutic interventions tailored to individual patients' genetic profiles [25].

The integration of molecular subtyping and genomic profiling into diagnostic and treatment protocols holds significant promise for enhancing the management of bladder cancer.This groundbreaking study aims to revolutionize bladder cancer diagnostics by harnessing the potential of methylation markers and single nucleotide polymorphism sites [26].Leveraging cuttingedge next-generation sequencing technologies, sophisticated bioinformatics algorithms, and rigorous validation protocols, the study meticulously identifies potential diagnostic biomarkers associated with urothelial bladder carcinoma.The development of this precise diagnostic tool holds immense promise in enhancing early detection rates, facilitating timely interventions, and ultimately improving patient outcomes [27] .

By delving into the cellular landscape of urothelial cancer and harnessing the power of genomic profiling, this study seeks to pave the way for the development of a highly accurate and targeted diagnostic tool.The utilization of methylation markers and SNP sites, in combination with advanced NGS technologies and bioinformatics algorithms, aims to identify specific biomarkers that can aid in the early and precise detection of UBC [28].The successful development and implementation of this diagnostic tool have the potential to transform the clinical management of UBC, offering healthcare professionals a sophisticated and reliable method for detecting and diagnosing this complex malignancy [29].Ultimately, this innovation has the capacity to significantly improve patient outcomes by enabling timely interventions and tailored treatment strategies.The etiological landscape of bladder cancer is multifaceted, shaped by a complex interplay of genetic predispositions, environmental exposures, and lifestyle factors.

Title: Analysis of urine cell-free DNA in bladder cancer diagnosis by emerging bioactive technologies and materials
Snippet: Mutations and accumulations within proto-oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes in somatic cells are critical hallmarks of malignant tumors. Like lung cancer and melanoma, bladder cancer exhibits high mutation rate, emerging as a malignancy with a significant mutational burden. Analyses of bladder cancer specimens revealed 302 mutations across exons, alterations within 204 copy number segments at the genomic level, and 20 instances of genomic rearrangements (Cancer Genome Atlas Research, 2014). Recent research has identified mutations in genes such as TP53, FGFR3, PIK3CA, MLL2, CDKN1A, and ERGC2 in patients with bladder cancer. These genetic aberrations play pivotal roles in essential physiological mechanisms, including cell cycle control and programmed cell death. Notably, alterations in the tumor suppressor gene TP53 are detectable in approximately half of the cases (Cancer Genome Atlas Research, 2014). As a critical driver gene in bladder cancer, TP53 inactivation disrupts normal cellular cycle checkpoints, fostering genomic instability that promotes tumorigenesis. Additionally, TP53 expression levels correlate with bladder cancer progression and serve as significant prognostic indicators (Hollstein et al., 1991). Alterations in FGFR3 also constitute critical mutations in bladder cancer, displaying strong associations with disease stage and grade; approximately 78.1% of patients with non-invasive bladder cancer showed FGFR3 expression, whereas the expression rate dropped to 18.2% in muscle-invasive cases (Akanksha and Sandhya, 2019). Thus, mutational profiles are salient biomarkers for bladder cancer, promising tools for tumor screening, diagnosis, and ongoing assessment to elucidate tumorigenic pathways. 

Obtaining tumor mutational data from tissue biopsies provides insights into cancer progression but is hindered by its invasive nature, which poses risks of complications and limits its use for longterm monitoring. Urine, readily accessible with minimal protein contamination and directly interacting with bladder cancer cells, is a preferable alternative. Numerous studies corroborate the high concordance between urine and tissue samples in terms of tumor DNA congruence (Ou et al., 2020;Zhang et al., 2021;Hirotsu et al., 2019).

Title: Genomic Characteristics of Bladder Cancer: An AACR Project GENIE Study
Snippet: Bladder and urothelial carcinoma are marked by profound genomic diversity. Using a large, multi-institutional dataset, we performed comprehensive genomic profiling of 4631 tumor samples from 4050 individuals. A retrospective analysis of bladder and urothelial cancer was performed using the AACR Project GENIE database. Demographic associations, mutation frequencies, copy number changes, and survival correlations were analyzed with a p-value < 0.05. Frequent mutations were identified in TP53, TERT, KDM6A, KMT2D, ARID1A, and FGFR3. Mutation frequencies varied by sex and race, with specific alterations enriched in female and Asian patients. Distinct patterns of co-occurrence, including TP53 with RB1, and mutual exclusivity, including TP53 with FGFR3 or KDM6A, revealed distinct molecular subtypes. This study highlights the extensive heterogeneity of bladder cancer, and our findings emphasize the clinical importance of molecular stratification and support the need for further mechanistic and prospective studies to inform the development of targeted therapies.

Title: Comprehensive genomic characterization of early-stage bladder cancer
Snippet: Understanding the molecular landscape of nonmuscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) is essential to improve risk assessment and treatment regimens. We performed a comprehensive genomic analysis of patients with NMIBC using whole-exome sequencing (n = 438), shallow whole-genome sequencing (n = 362) and total RNA sequencing (n = 414). A large genomic variation within NMIBC was observed and correlated with different molecular subtypes. Frequent loss of heterozygosity in FGFR3 and 17p (affecting TP53) was found in tumors with mutations in FGFR3 and TP53, respectively. Whole-genome doubling (WGD) was observed in 15% of the tumors and was associated with worse outcomes. Tumors with WGD were genomically unstable, with alterations in cell-cycle-related genes and an altered immune composition. Finally, integrative clustering of multi-omics data highlighted the important role of genomic instability and immune cell exhaustion in disease aggressiveness. These findings advance our understanding of genomic differences associated with disease aggressiveness in NMIBC and may ultimately improve patient stratification. A genomic and transcriptomic analysis of nonmuscle-invasive bladder cancer identifies four molecular subtypes, and associates whole-genome duplication and immune exhaustion with tumor progression.

Title: The UBC-40 Urothelial Bladder Cancer cell line index: a genomic resource for functional studies
Snippet: Urothelial bladder cancer is a highly heterogeneous disease. Cancer cell lines are useful tools for its study. This is a comprehensive genomic characterization of 40 urothelial bladder carcinoma (UBC) cell lines including information on origin, mutation status of genes implicated in bladder cancer (FGFR3, PIK3CA, TP53, and RAS), copy number alterations assessed using high density SNP arrays, uniparental disomy (UPD) events, and gene expression. Based on gene mutation patterns and genomic changes we identify lines representative of the FGFR3-driven tumor pathway and of the TP53/RB tumor suppressor-driven pathway. High-density array copy number analysis identified significant focal gains (1q32, 5p13.1-12, 7q11, and 7q33) and losses (i.e. 6p22.1) in regions altered in tumors but not previously described as affected in bladder cell lines. We also identify new evidence for frequent regions of UPD, often coinciding with regions reported to be lost in tumors. Previously undescribed chromosome X losses found in UBC lines also point to potential tumor suppressor genes. Cell lines representative of the FGFR3-driven pathway showed a lower number of UPD events. Overall, there is a predominance of more aggressive tumor subtypes among the cell lines. We provide a cell line classification that establishes their relatedness to the major molecularly-defined bladder tumor subtypes. The compiled information should serve as a useful reference to the bladder cancer research community and should help to select cell lines appropriate for the functional analysis of bladder cancer genes, for example those being identified through massive parallel sequencing.
