attempts.answer:
Overview and motivation
Bladder cancer’s genetic and epigenetic landscapes are heterogeneous yet structured enough to define clinically actionable subgroups and mechanistic opportunities. Across non–muscle–invasive (NMIBC) and muscle‑invasive (MIBC) disease, recurrent driver alterations cluster by disease stage—FGFR3 and PIK3CA mutations, loss of chromosome 9, and chromatin-remodeling gene aberrations are frequent in NMIBC, whereas TP53, RB1, and pathway alterations in RTK/RAS/PI3K are hallmark in MIBC; whole-exome/transcriptomic analyses further reveal APOBEC mutational signatures and strong concordance between localized and metastatic tumors, with luminal/basal/squamous/neuroendocrine transcriptomic subtypes showing distinct behavior and therapy-induced remodeling <cite id="9005b2aa-3">NMIBC is further characterized by frequent FGFR3 and PIK3CA mutations, loss of chromosome 9, and widespread chromatin-remodeling gene alterations</cite> <cite id="9005b2aa-3">MIBC displays high genomic instability, with recurrent mutations in TP53, RB1, and chromatin modifiers, as well as frequent alterations in the RTK/RAS/PI3K pathway</cite> <cite id="9005b2aa-3">In metastatic disease, NGS and whole-exome analyses reveal strong concordance with localized tumors, with frequent TP53, ARID1A, KMT2D, RB1, and FGFR3 alterations and APOBEC mutational signatures</cite> <cite id="9005b2aa-3">Consensus transcriptomic classifications identify reproducible molecular subtypes (luminal, basal/squamous, stroma rich, and neuroendocrine like), each with distinct biological and clinical behaviors</cite> <cite id="9005b2aa-3">Transcriptomic profiling shows subtype heterogeneity and therapy-induced remodeling</cite>. These patterns, alongside recurrent mutations in chromatin remodelers (KMT2D, KDM6A, ARID1A) that collectively occur in roughly 40–50% of tumors, provide mechanistic entry points for targeted agents and enable biomarker-driven risk stratification and trial selection <cite id="9005b2aa-2">Lines of evidence increasingly point to distinct genetic and epigenetic alteration patterns in bladder cancer, even between the different stages and grades of disease</cite> <cite id="9005b2aa-2">Genetic and epigenetic alterations have been demonstrated to play important roles during bladder tumorigenesis</cite> <cite id="9005b2aa-2">This review will focus on bladder cancer-associated genomic and epigenomic alterations, which are common in bladder cancer and provide potential diagnostic markers and therapeutic targets for bladder cancer treatment</cite> <cite id="2d7467aa-4">Bladder cancer is characterized by high rates of mutations within chromatin-modifying or chromatin-regulatory genes (44%)</cite>.

How the genetic and epigenetic landscapes enable precision medicine
1) Genomic subtyping to match biology and therapy
- Stage-specific landscapes support tailored strategies. FGFR3 and PIK3CA mutations with 9p loss in low‑grade papillary tumors align with targeted FGFR/PI3K approaches and conservative management, while TP53/RB1 alterations and RTK/RAS/PI3K pathway activation in MIBC point to cytotoxic chemotherapy, RTK inhibitors, or pathway-directed agents where feasible <cite id="9005b2aa-3">NMIBC is further characterized by frequent FGFR3 and PIK3CA mutations, loss of chromosome 9, and widespread chromatin-remodeling gene alterations</cite> <cite id="9005b2aa-3">MIBC displays high genomic instability, with recurrent mutations in TP53, RB1, and chromatin modifiers, as well as frequent alterations in the RTK/RAS/PI3K pathway</cite>. Transcriptomic subtypes (luminal, basal/squamous, stroma‑rich, neuroendocrine) have distinct prognoses and differential sensitivity to immune and targeted therapies, offering a framework for trial stratification and treatment selection <cite id="9005b2aa-3">Consensus transcriptomic classifications identify reproducible molecular subtypes (luminal, basal/squamous, stroma rich, and neuroendocrine like), each with distinct biological and clinical behaviors</cite> <cite id="9005b2aa-3">Transcriptomic profiling shows subtype heterogeneity and therapy-induced remodeling</cite>.
- Actionable FGFR addiction. FGFR3 alterations are prevalent in bladder cancer and often independent of TP53/RB1 mutations; these alterations drive a distinct FGFR-addicted phenotype that underpins approvals and combinations of FGFR inhibitors and antibody–drug conjugates, with erdafitinib approved as a targeted therapy and ongoing studies testing FGFR inhibitor–ICI combinations and earlier-stage applications <cite id="67ee77ff-2">FGFR3 mutations are particularly prevalent in BC, a heterogeneous form of UC, and account for a considerable proportion of new cancer diagnoses annually</cite> <cite id="67ee77ff-2">These FGFR genomic alterations often occur independently of mutations in other BC oncogenes, such as TP53 and RB1</cite> <cite id="67ee77ff-2">In 2019, erdafitinib became pivotal for the treatment of mUC, particularly in patients with specific FGFR alterations</cite> <cite id="67ee77ff-2">Recent studies have highlighted the benefits of combining erdafitinib with immunotherapy, thereby broadening the treatment options</cite> <cite id="67ee77ff-2">Ongoing investigations exist on its use in non-muscle-invasive BC and in combination with drugs such as enfortumab vedotin in mUC</cite>.
- ERBB2/HER2 as a precision target in the “mutated and amplified” subset. Across 2,035 genotyped tumors, ~14.5% of urothelial cancers harbor oncogenic ERBB2 alterations (6.7% mutation, 6.3% amplification, 1.5% co-mutation and amplification), and trastuzumab deruxtecan (T‑DXd) shows exceptional responses when ERBB2 co‑mutation and amplification co-occur; these insights support functional testing (organoids/xenografts) and precision oncology platforms to guide selection of HER2‑directed ADCs over TKIs in this heterogenous locus <cite id="0a7b9948-0">In an analysis of 42,415 prospectively analyzed solid tumors, we show that 14.5% of urothelial cancers have oncogenic or likely oncogenic ERBB2 alterations (6.7% ERBB2 mutation, 6.3% amplification of wildtype ERBB2, and 1.5% concurrent mutation and amplification)</cite> <cite id="0a7b9948-0">Patient-derived models show HER2-targeted ADC trastuzumab deruxtecan is significantly more effective than the HER kinase inhibitor neratinib</cite> <cite id="0a7b9948-0">In a real-world cohort, co-mutation and amplification of ERBB2 is associated with exceptional clinical response</cite> <cite id="0a7b9948-0">Discordance of ERBB2 mutational status between primary and metastatic disease sites is common in patients with urothelial cancer as is discordance of ERBB2 mutational status between patient-derived organoid/xenograft models and the tumors from which they were derived</cite> <cite id="0a7b9948-0">Our data support expanded clinical trials of HER2-targeted ADCs for urothelial cancers with low HER2 expression, the clinical testing of HER2 ADCs with alternative cytotoxic payloads, and the development of functional precision oncology platforms capable of assessing payload sensitivity pre-treatment as a guide to individualized therapy selection</cite>. Real‑world and pan‑tumor data further corroborate clinical activity in ERBB2‑mutant cases, though small response rates in unselected cohorts highlight the need for biomarker‑enriched trials <cite id="0a7b9948-1">The DESTINY-PanTumor01 study included 7 patients with urothelial cancer; the ORR was 29.4% pan-cancer with 2 of 7 patients with urothelial cancer achieving an objective response</cite>.
- Pathway-directed opportunities. Frequent RTK/RAS/PI3K pathway alterations in MIBC nominate TKIs and PI3K pathway modulators for rational combinations with or without immunotherapy; this is consistent with the emergence of targeted agents and combinations in metastatic disease, albeit with variable efficacy and the need for biomarker-defined subsets <cite id="9005b2aa-3">MIBC displays high genomic instability, with recurrent mutations in TP53, RB1, and chromatin modifiers, as well as frequent alterations in the RTK/RAS/PI3K pathway</cite> <cite id="67ee77ff-2">The treatment of metastatic urothelial cancer has transformed significantly with the introduction of diverse therapies, such as immune checkpoint inhibitors, targeted therapies, and antibody-drug conjugates</cite>.

2) Epigenetic remodeling as both driver and druggable layer
- Chromatin and DNA methylation define vulnerabilities. Mutations in chromatin remodelers (ARID1A, KMT2C/D, histone modifiers EZH2/CREBBP/EP300) are frequent and drive loss of nucleosome positioning, enhancer dysfunction, and transcriptional plasticity that shape intratumoral heterogeneity and immune evasion; these changes remodel the tumor microenvironment and modulate response to chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and targeted agents <cite id="2d7467aa-0">Mutations of chromatin remodeler ARID1A, KMT2C, KMT2D, and histone modifying enzymes (EP300, CREBBP and EZH2) lead to lack of nucleosome positioning, lack of enhancer function and transcriptional program perturbation, contributing to intratumoral heterogeneity and transcriptional plasticity resulting in failure in immunoevasion; these changes sculpt the tumor microenvironment and impact the response to chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and targeted therapy</cite>. Noninvasive epigenetic biomarkers (urine/plasma DNA methylation, chromatin accessibility) can stratify patients and monitor disease, complementing tissue genomics <cite id="2d7467aa-0">Epigenetic biomarkers based on mutation profiles, chromatin accessibility and DNA methylation signatures present new non-invasive strategies that can be followed for early detection, monitoring of disease and stratification of patients usage; which are all available in urine or plasma</cite>.
- Subtype-specific epigenetic dependencies. ARID1A-mutant bladder cancers exhibit synthetic vulnerability to EZH2 inhibition: ARID1A-deficient tumors show reduced viability, colony formation, and in vivo growth upon EZH2 blockade, supporting clinical testing of EZH2 inhibitors—alone or in combination with ICIs/chemotherapy—as precision strategies within the chromatin-mutant cohort <cite id="2d7467aa-3">ARID1A deficient tumors, but not ARID1A wild-type tumors are sensitive to EZH2 inhibition</cite> <cite id="2d7467aa-3">EZH2 inhibitor-treated ARID1A deficient bladder cancer cells show significantly reduced cell viability, colony formation, and in vivo tumor growth relative to ARID1A-wild type bladder cancer cells</cite>. Broader series confirm that KMT2D, KDM6A, and ARID1A are among the most common single-gene mutations and that KDM6A-null models are sensitive to EZH2 inhibition, reinforcing the therapeutic rationale for chromatin-targeted agents <cite id="2d7467aa-4">Key members of this family include KMT2D, KDM6A, and ARID1A, which account for the second, third, and fourth most commonly observed single gene mutations</cite> <cite id="2d7467aa-4">KDM6A-null bladder cancer cell lines were sensitive to EZH2 inhibition, making it an attractive therapeutic target</cite>.
- Immune microenvironment modulation by epigenetics. Epigenetic dysregulation (DNA methylation, histone modifications, non‑coding RNAs) is common and can act as driver events, enabling biomarker development and therapeutic targeting to enhance immunotherapy response; such epigenetic alterations provide mechanistic links between tumor biology and immunotherapy outcomes <cite id="2d7467aa-1">Aberrant DNA methylation, altered chromatin remodeling and deregulated expression of non-coding RNAs are common events in BC and can be driver events in BC pathogenesis, and are now being used as potential biomarkers and envisioned as potential therapeutic targets</cite> <cite id="2d7467aa-0">These changes sculpt the tumor microenvironment and impact the response to immunotherapy</cite>.
- Noninvasive liquid biopsy. Because epigenetic features can be captured in urine/plasma, they enable serial monitoring and early detection paradigms that complement tissue biopsies, potentially improving longitudinal precision and reducing sampling bias relative to relying solely on invasive resections <cite id="2d7467aa-0">Epigenetic biomarkers based on mutation profiles, chromatin accessibility and DNA methylation signatures present new non-invasive strategies that can be followed for early detection, monitoring of disease and stratification of patients usage; which are all available in urine or plasma</cite>.

3) Germline and tumor suppressor context: BRCA and chromatin modifier cohorts
- Germline BRCA1/2 loss and chromatin-mutant cohorts enrich for targeted options. High prevalence of chromatin regulator mutations supports targeted epigenetic therapies; frequent BRCA1/2 alterations nominate PARP inhibition, and combined chromatin/DDR blockade is a rational strategy under active investigation in precision oncology frameworks <cite id="2d7467aa-2">Mutations in chromatin remodelers (KDM6A, KMT2D, ARID1A, EP300) occur in ~ 80% of cases, driving transcriptional dysregulation and tumor progression</cite> <cite id="2d7467aa-2">Emerging evidence highlights novel PTMs in BCa pathogenesis; these aberrant PTMs offer therapeutic targets, including HDAC inhibitors and EZH2 modulators, with ongoing clinical trials exploring combination strategies</cite>. Clinically, FGFR3 alterations currently provide the clearest actionable guidance among validated biomarkers, anchoring trial arms and adaptive management in advanced disease <cite id="9005b2aa-3">Clinically, only FGFR3 alterations currently guide therapy</cite>.

4) Immunotherapy biomarkers: promise and pitfalls
- PD‑L1 and TMB can stratify benefit but are imperfect. Genomic instability and APOBEC signatures in metastatic disease align with immunogenicity, and PD‑L1 expression often correlates with response to checkpoint blockade; however, preanalytical variability (fixation/FFPE effects), intratumoral heterogeneity, dynamic evolution of PD‑L1 under therapy, and discordance between tissue and liquid biopsy complicate selection, leading to modest enrichment and the need for functional correlative assays and longitudinal sampling <cite id="9005b2aa-3">Transcriptomic profiling shows subtype heterogeneity and therapy-induced remodeling</cite> <cite id="9005b2aa-3">In metastatic disease, NGS and whole-exome analyses reveal strong concordance with localized tumors, with frequent TP53, ARID1A, KMT2D, RB1, and FGFR3 alterations and APOBEC mutational signatures</cite> <cite id="2d7467aa-0">These changes sculpt the tumor microenvironment and impact the response to immunotherapy</cite>. Early detection biomarkers often leverage methylation signatures detectable in urine or plasma, yet their translation to selection biomarkers is hindered by sampling bias (urothelial epithelium vs invasive disease), fixation-induced DNA/RNA degradation, and assay mismatch to the pharmacodynamic endpoints of targeted agents or immune checkpoint pathways <cite id="2d7467aa-0">Epigenetic biomarkers based on mutation profiles, chromatin accessibility and DNA methylation signatures present new non-invasive strategies that can be followed for early detection, monitoring of disease and stratification of patients usage; which are all available in urine or plasma</cite> <cite id="2d7467aa-0">These changes sculpt the tumor microenvironment and impact the response to chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and targeted therapy</cite>.

Why early‑detection biomarkers often fail to translate to treatment selection
1) Biological heterogeneity and clonal evolution
- Spatial and temporal heterogeneity. Within-patient tumor evolution creates discordance between primary and metastatic lesions and between models and patient tumors; ERBB2 status often shifts across disease sites and fails to be faithfully recapitulated in organoid/xenografts, undermining biomarker–drug matching at the time of first biopsy or model-guided selection <cite id="0a7b9948-0">Discordance of ERBB2 mutational status between primary and metastatic disease sites is common in patients with urothelial cancer as is discordance of ERBB2 mutational status between patient-derived organoid/xenograft models and the tumors from which they were derived</cite>. Transcriptomic profiling shows therapy-induced remodeling, meaning baseline biomarkers may no longer reflect resistance-conferring alterations that emerge under treatment <cite id="9005b2aa-3">Transcriptomic profiling shows subtype heterogeneity and therapy-induced remodeling</cite>.
- Subtype-specific biology. Luminal versus basal/squamous programs respond differently to targeted and immune therapies; early-detection biomarkers optimized for prevalence (e.g., papillary luminal disease) may miss molecular drivers in de novo basal/squamous or neuroendocrine derivatives, leading to poor predictive accuracy for systemic treatments <cite id="9005b2aa-3">Consensus transcriptomic classifications identify reproducible molecular subtypes (luminal, basal/squamous, stroma rich, and neuroendocrine like), each with distinct biological and clinical behaviors</cite>.

2) Sampling and pre-analytical bias
- Tissue source and invasiveness. Early detection relies on minimally invasive urine or fine-needle aspirate samples, which may underrepresent invasive, immune‑hot MIBC phenotypes and miss actionable alterations present in muscle layers; fixation and processing affect DNA/RNA integrity and protein epitopes, altering PD‑L1, methylation, and mutation calling fidelity compared with optimally processed FFPE or fresh frozen blocks <cite id="2d7467aa-0">These changes sculpt the tumor microenvironment and impact the response to chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and targeted therapy</cite> <cite id="2d7467aa-0">Epigenetic biomarkers based on mutation profiles, chromatin accessibility and DNA methylation signatures present new non-invasive strategies that can be followed for early detection, monitoring of disease and stratification of patients usage; which are all available in urine or plasma</cite>. Chromatin and enhancer dysregulation complicate interpretation of tissue-based assays that assume stable chromatin states at time of sampling <cite id="2d7467aa-0">Mutations of chromatin remodeler ... lead to lack of enhancer function and ... transcriptional plasticity resulting in failure in immunoevasion</cite>.
- Model–tumor discordance. Patient-derived models frequently diverge at the target locus (e.g., ERBB2) from the original tumor and metastases, producing false-positive or negative predictions and misallocation to targeted agents without matched genomic context <cite id="0a7b9948-0">Discordance of ERBB2 mutational status between primary and metastatic disease sites is common ... as is discordance ... between patient-derived organoid/xenograft models and the tumors</cite>.

3) Assay mismatch and validation pitfalls
- Pharmacodynamic vs predictive biomarkers. Biomarkers optimized for early detection (e.g., mutation presence or methylation signal) may not map onto the drug’s pharmacodynamic effect. For example, FGFR3 mutation is prevalent but does not directly predict FGFR inhibitor sensitivity; instead, functional FGFR pathway activation and copy-number amplification inform selection for FGFR inhibitors and ADCs like enfortumab vedotin, which has shown clear clinical activity in FGFR-altered cohorts and combinations <cite id="67ee77ff-2">Erdafitinib became pivotal for the treatment of mUC, particularly in patients with specific FGFR alterations</cite> <cite id="67ee77ff-2">Ongoing investigations exist on its use in non-muscle-invasive BC and in combination with drugs such as enfortumab vedotin</cite> <cite id="0a7b9948-0">Co-mutation and amplification of ERBB2 is associated with exceptional response to T-DXd</cite>. PD‑L1 immunohistochemistry is influenced by tumor microenvironment composition and pre-analytical conditions; dynamic remodeling under therapy means baseline IHC may not forecast benefit, and liquid biopsy discordance further erodes predictive accuracy <cite id="9005b2aa-3">Transcriptomic profiling shows subtype heterogeneity and therapy-induced remodeling</cite> <cite id="2d7467aa-0">These changes sculpt the tumor microenvironment and impact the response to immunotherapy</cite>.
- Overfitting to prevalence and rarity bias. Early detection studies often enroll NMIBC (with FGFR3/PIK3CA predominance), while systemic treatment selection concerns MIBC with TP53/RB1/RTK alterations; training biomarkers on detection-relevant cohorts leads to poor generalization to therapy-relevant disease biology <cite id="9005b2aa-3">NMIBC is further characterized by frequent FGFR3 and PIK3CA mutations ... MIBC displays high genomic instability, with recurrent mutations in TP53, RB1, and chromatin modifiers, as well as frequent alterations in the RTK/RAS/PI3K pathway</cite>.

4) Clinical utility requires prospective, functional validation
- Biomarker-to-drug mapping needs functional assays. Precision medicine requires linking biomarkers to functional sensitivity via preclinical models and early-phase trials; in urothelial cancer, trastuzumab deruxtecan’s clinical activity in ERBB2 co‑mutant/amplified cases and greater potency than neratinib in models justify functional testing (e.g., organoids) to guide therapy rather than relying solely on germline detection pipelines or expression IHC <cite id="0a7b9948-0">Patient-derived urothelial cancer models, the HER2-targeted ADC trastuzumab deruxtecan is significantly more effective than the HER kinase inhibitor neratinib</cite> <cite id="0a7b9948-0">Our data support ... development of functional precision oncology platforms capable of assessing payload sensitivity pre-treatment as a guide to individualized therapy selection</cite>. For chromatin-driven disease, targeting EZH2 or HDAC/CREBBP axes in ARID1A/KDM6A-mutant subsets shows preclinical and early clinical rationale, but dosing, combinations, and predictive signatures still need prospective validation tied to response biomarkers and toxicity control <cite id="2d7467aa-3">ARID1A deficient tumors ... are sensitive to EZH2 inhibition</cite> <cite id="2d7467aa-2">These aberrant PTMs offer therapeutic targets, including HDAC inhibitors and EZH2 modulators, with ongoing clinical trials exploring combination strategies</cite>.

- Genomic detection success stories vs failures. Title: FGFR Inhibitors in Urothelial Cancer: From Scientific Rationale to Clinical Development
Snippet: In the past decade, the treatment of metastatic urothelial cancer (mUC), including bladder cancer (BC), has transformed significantly with the introduction of diverse therapies, such as immune checkpoint inhibitors, targeted therapies, and antibody-drug conjugates. This change is partly due to advancements in genomic understanding, particularly next-generation sequencing, which has identified numerous mutations in UC. Among these therapies, erdafitinib, a pan-fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) inhibitor for specific FGFR2 and FGFR3 alterations, is the only targeted therapy approved till now. In 2019, erdafitinib became pivotal for the treatment of mUC, particularly in patients with specific FGFR alterations. Recent studies have highlighted the benefits of combining erdafitinib with immunotherapy, thereby broadening the treatment options. Ongoing investigations exist on its use in non-muscle-invasive BC and in combination with drugs such as enfortumab vedotin in mUC. Other FGFR-targeted agents are under development; however, overcoming FGFR resistance and ensuring the safety of combination therapies remain major hurdles. FGFR3 mutations are particularly prevalent in BC, a heterogeneous form of UC, and account for a considerable proportion of new cancer diagnoses annually. Approximately half of these cancers have FGFR3 mutations, with gene rearrangements being a common feature. These FGFR3 genomic alterations often occur independently of mutations in other BC oncogenes, such as TP53 and RB1. This review emphasizes the importance of FGFR inhibition in UC and the optimization of its use in clinical practice. Moreover, it underscores the ongoing efforts to evaluate combination strategies and early treatment testing to enhance the effectiveness of targeted therapies for UC.
</snippet>

Title: Epigenetics of Bladder Cancer: Where Biomarkers and Therapeutic Targets Meet
Snippet: Bladder cancer (BC) is the most common neoplasia of the urothelial tract. Due to its high incidence, prevalence, recurrence and mortality, it remains an unsolved clinical and social problem. The treatment of BC is challenging and, although immunotherapies have revealed potential benefit in a percentage of patients, it remains mostly an incurable disease at its advanced state. Epigenetic alterations, including aberrant DNA methylation, altered chromatin remodeling and deregulated expression of non-coding RNAs are common events in BC and can be driver events in BC pathogenesis. Accordingly, these epigenetic alterations are now being used as potential biomarkers for these disorders and are being envisioned as potential therapeutic targets for the future management of BC. In this review, we summarize the recent findings in these emerging and exciting new aspects paving the way for future clinical treatment of this disease.

Title: HDAC2 as a therapeutic target in bladder cancer: insights into the altered epigenetic regulation and lysine lactylation
Snippet: Bladder cancer (BCa) remains a major global health challenge, ranking as the ninth most common malignancy worldwide, with 573,000 new cases and 213,000 deaths annually [1]. It exhibits a strong male predominance (3-4 times higher incidence in men than women), with peak occurrence after age 60-70. Approximately 75% of cases are non-muscle-invasive (NMIBC), typically managed with transurethral resection and intravesical therapy (e.g., BCG or chemotherapy), while muscle-invasive (MIBC) and metastatic disease require radical cystectomy, radiotherapy, or systemic therapies [2]. Despite treatment advances, the 5-year survival remains highly stage-dependent, ranging from >80% for localized disease to < 40% for metastatic cases [3]. Recent therapeutic innovations, such as immune checkpoint inhibitors (e.g., pembrolizumab) and antibody-drug conjugates (e.g., enfortumab vedotin), have improved outcomes in advanced disease [4]. However, high intertumoral heterogeneity leads to vastly divergent responses among patients, which underscores the urgent need to explore novel pathogenic mechanisms and to develop strategies for improving sensitivity to standard therapies. 

BCa exhibits extensive epigenetic alterations, including DNA methylation, histone modifications, and non-coding RNA dysregulation [5]. Notably, mutations in chromatin remodelers (KDM6A, KMT2D, ARID1A, EP300) occur in ~ 80% of cases [6], driving transcriptional dysregulation and tumor progression. Emerging evidence highlights novel protein post-translational modifications (PTMs), such as lactylation (Kla) [7], S-palmitoylation [8] and SUMOylation [9] in BCa pathogenesis. These aberrant PTMs offer therapeutic targets, including HDAC inhibitors and EZH2 modulators, with ongoing clinical trials exploring combination strategies [10,11].

Title: ARID1A-mutant and deficient bladder cancer is sensitive to EZH2 pharmacologic inhibition
Snippet: Metastatic urothelial carcinoma of the bladder is generally incurable by current systemic therapy. Molecular characterization of bladder cancer (BLCa) has revealed multiple candidate driver genes for BLCa tumorigenesis. Epigenetic/chromatin modifiers have been shown to be frequently mutated in BLCa, with ARID1A mutations highly prevalent in nearly 20% of early and late stage tumors. EZH2 is a histone methyltransferase that acts as an oncogene. The data herein show that ARID1A deficient tumors, but not ARID1A wild-type tumors are sensitive to EZH2 inhibition. Specifically, EZH2 inhibitor-treated ARID1A deficient bladder cancer cells show significantly reduced cell viability, colony formation, and in vivo tumor growth relative to ARID1A-wild type bladder cancer cells. Thus, our study suggests that a specific subset of bladder cancer patients with ARID1A mutations can be therapeutically treated with pharmacologic inhibitors targeting EZH2.

Title: Determinants of sensitivity to HER2-targeted antibody drug conjugates in urothelial cancer
Snippet: HER2, encoded by the ERBB2 gene, is a receptor tyrosine kinase frequently activated in human cancers via gene amplification, mutation, and/or protein overexpression. In an analysis of 42,415 prospectively analyzed solid tumors, we show that 14.5% of urothelial cancers (n = 295/2,035) have oncogenic or likely oncogenic ERBB2 alterations (6.7% ERBB2 mutation, 6.3% amplification of wildtype ERBB2, and 1.5% concurrent mutation and amplification). Discordance of ERBB2 mutational status between primary and metastatic disease sites is common in patients with urothelial cancer as is discordance of ERBB2 mutational status between patient-derived organoid/xenograft models and the tumors from which they were derived. In patient-derived urothelial cancer models, the HER2-targeted antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) trastuzumab deruxtecan is significantly more effective than the HER kinase inhibitor neratinib. In a real-world cohort of patients with urothelial cancer treated with trastuzumab deruxtecan, co-mutation and amplification of ERBB2 is associated with exceptional clinical response. Our data support expanded clinical trials of HER2-targeted ADCs for urothelial cancers with low HER2 expression, the clinical testing of HER2 ADCs with alternative cytotoxic payloads, and the development of functional precision oncology platforms capable of assessing payload sensitivity pre-treatment as a guide to individualized therapy selection. Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) is a HER2-targeted antibody drug conjugate. Through integrated laboratory and clinical studies, the authors identify significant ERBB2 (the gene that encodes the HER2 protein) mutational heterogeneity in patients with urothelial cancer and co-mutation and amplification of ERBB2 as a potential biomarker of exceptional response to T-DXd.
</snippet>

Title: Determinants of sensitivity to HER2-targeted antibody drug conjugates in urothelial cancer
Snippet: This manuscript investigates the landscape and significance of ERBB2 alterations in urothelial cancers using a large cohort of 2,035 patients with tumor genomic profiling data. The authors develop and biologically characterize novel patient-derived bladder cancer models with HER2 alterations, and assess their in vivo sensitivity to trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd). These preclinical findings are complemented by data from a real-world clinical cohort of 28 patients with metastatic urothelial cancer treated with T-DXd. This is a timely and relevant study that provides valuable insights into HER2 biology and therapeutic response to HER2-targeted drugs in urothelial cancer. We offer the following comments and suggestions to help improve the quality of the manuscript: Introduction and Discussion: 1. Given that the manuscript addresses both HER2 amplification and mutations, we recommend broader discussion of the clinical data on HER2-mutant tumors treated with T-DXd. In particular, consider integrating findings from DESTINY-PanTumor01 (Li et al., Lancet Oncology, 2024), which includes 7 patients with HER2-mutant urothelial carcinoma. 

As suggested by the reviewer, we have revised the manuscript to include additional discussion of recently reported clinical data with T-DXd pan-cancer including specific references to and discussion of the DESTINY-PanTumor01 (Li et al., Lancet Oncology, 2024) study 4 . As highlighted by the reviewer, this study included 7 patients with urothelial cancer. The ORR was 29.4% pan-cancer with 2 of 7 patients with urothelial cancer achieving an objective response. While these results were promising, the results suggested the need for further studies to define the role of T-DXd in patients with urothelial cancer whose tumors harbor ERBB2 mutations, a goal of our real-world analyses in Figure 6. We thus believe that our current study provides further support for targeting HER2 with ADCs in patients with urothelial cancers, in particular, those with ERBB2 mutation and amplification, points we have sought to better highlight in the revised discussion.

Title: Phase II study of a trastuzumab biosimilar in combination with paclitaxel for HER2-positive recurrent or metastatic urothelial carcinoma: KCSG GU18-18
Snippet: Platinum-based combination therapy is the standard first-line treatment for metastatic urothelial carcinoma (UC). 1 Although the treatment outcomes of patients with metastatic UC who progress after first-line treatment have improved, a significant number of patients still show poor prognosis. 2,3ecent advances in molecular profiling techniques have facilitated the application of targeted therapies for the management of various tumors, including UC. Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), encoded by the ERBB2 gene, is one of the most extensively studied therapeutic targets in solid tumors.HER2-driven tumorigenesis can occur via multiple mechanisms, including ERBB2 amplification, ERBB2 mutation, and HER2 protein overexpression.A comprehensive analysis of molecular alterations in 131 muscle-invasive, high-grade urothelial bladder cancers was carried out in The Cancer Genome Atlas project, which led to the identification of 32 recurrent mutations. 4Of the genomic alterations identified, ERBB2 mutation or amplification, which could offer potential targets for HER2-directed therapy, was found in 9% of the UC cases.In another genomic profiling study of 295 cases of advanced UC of the bladder, ERBB2 genomic alteration was one of the most common events (17%). 5The incidence of HER2 overexpression ranges from 0% to 25% in patients with UC; 6 however, the prognostic value of HER2 in UC is unknown.

Clinical trials of HER2-targeting agents have been conducted in patients with advanced UC; however, the results are controversial.Trastuzumab, a monoclonal antibody against HER2, resulted in an objective response rate (ORR) of 70% with a median time to progression of 9.3 months in advanced HER2-positive UC when used as first-line therapy in combination with paclitaxel, carboplatin, and gemcitabine. 7In contrast, addition of trastuzumab to gemcitabine plus platinum did not lead to significant clinical benefit in terms of both ORR and survival in patients with advanced UC overexpressing HER2. 8

Title: Molecular Correlates of In Vitro Responses to Dacomitinib and Afatinib in Bladder Cancer
Snippet: Bladder cancer is predicted to have over 79,000 new cases and cause over 16,000 deaths in 2017. It is the second most common genitourinary cancer, fourth most common cancer in men, and the eighth highest cause of cancer death in men [1]. Mortality for invasive and metastatic bladder cancer remains high [2]. The recent observations of impressive and durable responses to new immune therapies were the first improvement in metastatic bladder cancer treatments in the past 20 years. However, responses to these promising new agents are limited to 20-30 percent of patients [3]. New and more effective treatments as well as predictive and prognostic markers must be found. 

Precision medicine, which matches targeted therapies to the individual molecular profile of a patients' tumor, has shown promise in many tumor types [4]. For bladder cancer, members of the HER/erbB family have been recognized as potential targets. The HER family includes four proteins: HER1/epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR); HER2/erbB2; HER 3; and HER 4. Of these four proteins, three (EGFR, HER2 and HER4) have intracellular portions capable of cell signaling, while HER3 lacks active intracellular kinase domains. In response to ligand binding, members of this family form dimers which activate a tyrosine kinase signaling cascade [5][6][7]. 

EGFR overexpression has long been observed in bladder cancer, and appears to contribute to progression and invasion in bladder cancer [8]. HER2 expression has been reported in bladder cancer, and some studies suggest expression may be associated with more aggressive metastatic disease and shorter survival [9][10][11]. The Cancer Genome Atlas Project identified amplification in EGFR, amplification and mutation in HER2, and/or HER3 in multiple muscleinvasive bladder cancer tumors. Additionally, these alterations were mostly found in different tumors, which results in nearly 20% of patients demonstrating alteration in one of these genes [12]. These results have been confirmed in an independent study [13]. In spite of these data, early clinical trials targeting either EGFR or HER2 were mixed.
</snippet>

Title: Diverse ERBB2/ERBB3 Activating Alterations and Coalterations Have Implications for HER2/3-Targeted Therapies across Solid Tumors
Snippet: Genomic profiling has identified ERBB2 amplification and mutations, encoding overexpressed or hyperactivated HER2, and ERBB3 (encoding HER3) alterations as drivers of human cancers (1). When ERBB2 (HER2) is amplified or mutated, it becomes activated in a ligand-independent manner, driving activation of downstream pathways controlling the migration, proliferation, survival, and differentiation of cancer cells (1). Multiple HER2targeted therapies have been approved to treat HER2 amplification and/or overexpression in breast cancer via different mechanisms of action, including monoclonal antibodies (mAb; e.g., trastuzumab), tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI, e.g., neratinib), and antibody-drug conjugates [ADC, e.g., trastuzumab emtansine and trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd); ref . 2]. 

Trastuzumab and T-DXd are also approved for the treatment of HER2amplified and/or -overexpressed gastric cancers (3). In the last 2 years, T-DXd was approved to treat non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with select ERBB2 mutations (4), and tucatinib plus trastuzumab was approved to treat HER2 amplification and/or overexpression in colorectal cancer (CRC) (5). Most recently, T-DXd received pan-tumor approval for unresectable or metastatic HER2-overexpressing (IHC 3+) solid tumors (6)(7)(8). 

Recent trials investigating HER2-targeted therapies have demonstrated efficacy in solid tumors with ERBB2 (HER2) alterations in indications which have not been approved by the U.S. FDA (9). Specifically, the lack of approved HER2-targeted therapies for non-NSCLC with ERBB2 mutations in the absence of amplification/overexpression suggests an unmet clinical need for a substantial population of patients (10,11).

- Spatial and temporal heterogeneity. Title: Genetic and Epigenetic Alterations in Bladder Cancer
Snippet: Bladder cancer is one of the most common cancers worldwide, with a high rate of recurrence and poor outcomes as a result of relapse. Title: FGFR Inhibitors in Urothelial Cancer: From Scientific Rationale to Clinical Development
Snippet: In the past decade, the treatment of metastatic urothelial cancer (mUC), including bladder cancer (BC), has transformed significantly with the introduction of diverse therapies, such as immune checkpoint inhibitors, targeted therapies, and antibody-drug conjugates. This change is partly due to advancements in genomic understanding, particularly next-generation sequencing, which has identified numerous mutations in UC. Among these therapies, erdafitinib, a pan-fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) inhibitor for specific FGFR2 and FGFR3 alterations, is the only targeted therapy approved till now. In 2019, erdafitinib became pivotal for the treatment of mUC, particularly in patients with specific FGFR alterations. Recent studies have highlighted the benefits of combining erdafitinib with immunotherapy, thereby broadening the treatment options. Ongoing investigations exist on its use in non-muscle-invasive BC and in combination with drugs such as enfortumab vedotin in mUC. Other FGFR-targeted agents are under development; however, overcoming FGFR resistance and ensuring the safety of combination therapies remain major hurdles. FGFR3 mutations are particularly prevalent in BC, a heterogeneous form of UC, and account for a considerable proportion of new cancer diagnoses annually. Approximately half of these cancers have FGFR3 mutations, with gene rearrangements being a common feature. These FGFR3 genomic alterations often occur independently of mutations in other BC oncogenes, such as TP53 and RB1. This review emphasizes the importance of FGFR inhibition in UC and the optimization of its use in clinical practice. Moreover, it underscores the ongoing efforts to evaluate combination strategies and early treatment testing to enhance the effectiveness of targeted therapies for UC.

Title: Epigenetic Alterations and Chromatin Landscape Remodeling in Urothelial Bladder Cancer: Molecular Drivers, Biomarker Potential, and Emerging Therapeutic Strategies
Snippet: Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder (UBC) is a heterogeneous disease from the clinicopathologic and molecular standpoint and presents clinical management problems for its range in progression, frequent recurrence and complicated genetic/epigenetic architecture. Not only traditional genetic changes, but also epigenetic dysregulation (e.g., alterations of chromatin remodeling, histone modification and DNA methylation) has been increasingly recognized to play a pivotal role in the process of tumor initiation, progression, metastasis and resistance to therapy. It is a dissapointing result that mutations of the chromatin remodeler such as ARID1A, KMT2C, KMT2D, and histone modifying enzymes (EP300, CREBBP and EZH2) not only cause loss-of-nucleosome positioning in addition lead to lack of enhancer function and perturbation ofT program contributing to shaping up intratumoral heterogeneity as well as transcriptional plasticity resulting in failure in immunoevasion. Title: Determinants of sensitivity to HER2-targeted antibody drug conjugates in urothelial cancer
Snippet: HER2, encoded by the ERBB2 gene, is a receptor tyrosine kinase frequently activated in human cancers via gene amplification, mutation, and/or protein overexpression. In an analysis of 42,415 prospectively analyzed solid tumors, we show that 14.5% of urothelial cancers (n = 295/2,035) have oncogenic or likely oncogenic ERBB2 alterations (6.7% ERBB2 mutation, 6.3% amplification of wildtype ERBB2, and 1.5% concurrent mutation and amplification). Discordance of ERBB2 mutational status between primary and metastatic disease sites is common in patients with urothelial cancer as is discordance of ERBB2 mutational status between patient-derived organoid/xenograft models and the tumors from which they were derived. In patient-derived urothelial cancer models, the HER2-targeted antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) trastuzumab deruxtecan is significantly more effective than the HER kinase inhibitor neratinib. In a real-world cohort of patients with urothelial cancer treated with trastuzumab deruxtecan, co-mutation and amplification of ERBB2 is associated with exceptional clinical response. Our data support expanded clinical trials of HER2-targeted ADCs for urothelial cancers with low HER2 expression, the clinical testing of HER2 ADCs with alternative cytotoxic payloads, and the development of functional precision oncology platforms capable of assessing payload sensitivity pre-treatment as a guide to individualized therapy selection. Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) is a HER2-targeted antibody drug conjugate. Through integrated laboratory and clinical studies, the authors identify significant ERBB2 (the gene that encodes the HER2 protein) mutational heterogeneity in patients with urothelial cancer and co-mutation and amplification of ERBB2 as a potential biomarker of exceptional response to T-DXd.

Title: Determinants of sensitivity to HER2-targeted antibody drug conjugates in urothelial cancer
Snippet: This manuscript investigates the landscape and significance of ERBB2 alterations in urothelial cancers using a large cohort of 2,035 patients with tumor genomic profiling data. The authors develop and biologically characterize novel patient-derived bladder cancer models with HER2 alterations, and assess their in vivo sensitivity to trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd). These preclinical findings are complemented by data from a real-world clinical cohort of 28 patients with metastatic urothelial cancer treated with T-DXd. This is a timely and relevant study that provides valuable insights into HER2 biology and therapeutic response to HER2-targeted drugs in urothelial cancer. We offer the following comments and suggestions to help improve the quality of the manuscript: Introduction and Discussion: 1. Given that the manuscript addresses both HER2 amplification and mutations, we recommend broader discussion of the clinical data on HER2-mutant tumors treated with T-DXd. In particular, consider integrating findings from DESTINY-PanTumor01 (Li et al., Lancet Oncology, 2024), which includes 7 patients with HER2-mutant urothelial carcinoma. 

As suggested by the reviewer, we have revised the manuscript to include additional discussion of recently reported clinical data with T-DXd pan-cancer including specific references to and discussion of the DESTINY-PanTumor01 (Li et al., Lancet Oncology, 2024) study 4 . As highlighted by the reviewer, this study included 7 patients with urothelial cancer. The ORR was 29.4% pan-cancer with 2 of 7 patients with urothelial cancer achieving an objective response. While these results were promising, the results suggested the need for further studies to define the role of T-DXd in patients with urothelial cancer whose tumors harbor ERBB2 mutations, a goal of our real-world analyses in Figure 6. We thus believe that our current study provides further support for targeting HER2 with ADCs in patients with urothelial cancers, in particular, those with ERBB2 mutation and amplification, points we have sought to better highlight in the revised discussion.

Title: Phase II study of a trastuzumab biosimilar in combination with paclitaxel for HER2-positive recurrent or metastatic urothelial carcinoma: KCSG GU18-18
Snippet: Platinum-based combination therapy is the standard first-line treatment for metastatic urothelial carcinoma (UC). 1 Although the treatment outcomes of patients with metastatic UC who progress after first-line treatment have improved, a significant number of patients still show poor prognosis. 2,3ecent advances in molecular profiling techniques have facilitated the application of targeted therapies for the management of various tumors, including UC. Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), encoded by the ERBB2 gene, is one of the most extensively studied therapeutic targets in solid tumors.HER2-driven tumorigenesis can occur via multiple mechanisms, including ERBB2 amplification, ERBB2 mutation, and HER2 protein overexpression.A comprehensive analysis of molecular alterations in 131 muscle-invasive, high-grade urothelial bladder cancers was carried out in The Cancer Genome Atlas project, which led to the identification of 32 recurrent mutations. 4Of the genomic alterations identified, ERBB2 mutation or amplification, which could offer potential targets for HER2-directed therapy, was found in 9% of the UC cases.In another genomic profiling study of 295 cases of advanced UC of the bladder, ERBB2 genomic alteration was one of the most common events (17%). 5The incidence of HER2 overexpression ranges from 0% to 25% in patients with UC; 6 however, the prognostic value of HER2 in UC is unknown.

Clinical trials of HER2-targeting agents have been conducted in patients with advanced UC; however, the results are controversial.Trastuzumab, a monoclonal antibody against HER2, resulted in an objective response rate (ORR) of 70% with a median time to progression of 9.3 months in advanced HER2-positive UC when used as first-line therapy in combination with paclitaxel, carboplatin, and gemcitabine. 7In contrast, addition of trastuzumab to gemcitabine plus platinum did not lead to significant clinical benefit in terms of both ORR and survival in patients with advanced UC overexpressing HER2. 8

Title: Molecular Correlates of In Vitro Responses to Dacomitinib and Afatinib in Bladder Cancer
Snippet: Bladder cancer is predicted to have over 79,000 new cases and cause over 16,000 deaths in 2017. It is the second most common genitourinary cancer, fourth most common cancer in men, and the eighth highest cause of cancer death in men [1]. Mortality for invasive and metastatic bladder cancer remains high [2]. The recent observations of impressive and durable responses to new immune therapies were the first improvement in metastatic bladder cancer treatments in the past 20 years. However, responses to these promising new agents are limited to 20-30 percent of patients [3]. New and more effective treatments as well as predictive and prognostic markers must be found. 

Precision medicine, which matches targeted therapies to the individual molecular profile of a patients' tumor, has shown promise in many tumor types [4]. For bladder cancer, members of the HER/erbB family have been recognized as potential targets. The HER family includes four proteins: HER1/epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR); HER2/erbB2; HER 3; and HER 4. Of these four proteins, three (EGFR, HER2 and HER4) have intracellular portions capable of cell signaling, while HER3 lacks active intracellular kinase domains. In response to ligand binding, members of this family form dimers which activate a tyrosine kinase signaling cascade [5][6][7]. 

EGFR overexpression has long been observed in bladder cancer, and appears to contribute to progression and invasion in bladder cancer [8]. HER2 expression has been reported in bladder cancer, and some studies suggest expression may be associated with more aggressive metastatic disease and shorter survival [9][10][11]. The Cancer Genome Atlas Project identified amplification in EGFR, amplification and mutation in HER2, and/or HER3 in multiple muscleinvasive bladder cancer tumors. Additionally, these alterations were mostly found in different tumors, which results in nearly 20% of patients demonstrating alteration in one of these genes [12]. These results have been confirmed in an independent study [13]. In spite of these data, early clinical trials targeting either EGFR or HER2 were mixed.

Title: Diverse ERBB2/ERBB3 Activating Alterations and Coalterations Have Implications for HER2/3-Targeted Therapies across Solid Tumors
Snippet: Genomic profiling has identified ERBB2 amplification and mutations, encoding overexpressed or hyperactivated HER2, and ERBB3 (encoding HER3) alterations as drivers of human cancers (1). When ERBB2 (HER2) is amplified or mutated, it becomes activated in a ligand-independent manner, driving activation of downstream pathways controlling the migration, proliferation, survival, and differentiation of cancer cells (1). Multiple HER2targeted therapies have been approved to treat HER2 amplification and/or overexpression in breast cancer via different mechanisms of action, including monoclonal antibodies (mAb; e.g., trastuzumab), tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI, e.g., neratinib), and antibody-drug conjugates [ADC, e.g., trastuzumab emtansine and trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd); ref . 2]. 

Trastuzumab and T-DXd are also approved for the treatment of HER2amplified and/or -overexpressed gastric cancers (3). In the last 2 years, T-DXd was approved to treat non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with select ERBB2 mutations (4), and tucatinib plus trastuzumab was approved to treat HER2 amplification and/or overexpression in colorectal cancer (CRC) (5). Most recently, T-DXd received pan-tumor approval for unresectable or metastatic HER2-overexpressing (IHC 3+) solid tumors (6)(7)(8). 

Recent trials investigating HER2-targeted therapies have demonstrated efficacy in solid tumors with ERBB2 (HER2) alterations in indications which have not been approved by the U.S. FDA (9). Specifically, the lack of approved HER2-targeted therapies for non-NSCLC with ERBB2 mutations in the absence of amplification/overexpression suggests an unmet clinical need for a substantial population of patients (10,11).

snippet.text:
Bladder cancer is predicted to have over 79,000 new cases and cause over 16,000 deaths in 2017. It is the second most common genitourinary cancer, fourth most common cancer in men, and the eighth highest cause of cancer death in men [1]. Mortality for invasive and metastatic bladder cancer remains high [2]. The recent observations of impressive and durable responses to new immune therapies were the first improvement in metastatic bladder cancer treatments in the past 20 years. However, responses to these promising new agents are limited to 20-30 percent of patients [3]. New and more effective treatments as well as predictive and prognostic markers must be found. 

Precision medicine, which matches targeted therapies to the individual molecular profile of a patients' tumor, has shown promise in many tumor types [4]. For bladder cancer, members of the HER/erbB family have been recognized as potential targets. The HER family includes four proteins: HER1/epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR); HER2/erbB2; HER 3; and HER 4. Of these four proteins, three (EGFR, HER2 and HER4) have intracellular portions capable of cell signaling, while HER3 lacks active intracellular kinase domains. In response to ligand binding, members of this family form dimers which activate a tyrosine kinase signaling cascade [5][6][7]. 

EGFR overexpression has long been observed in bladder cancer, and appears to contribute to progression and invasion in bladder cancer [8]. HER2 expression has been reported in bladder cancer, and some studies suggest expression may be associated with more aggressive metastatic disease and shorter survival [9][10][11]. The Cancer Genome Atlas Project identified amplification in EGFR, amplification and mutation in HER2, and/or HER3 in multiple muscleinvasive bladder cancer tumors. Additionally, these alterations were mostly found in different tumors, which results in nearly 20% of patients demonstrating alteration in one of these genes [12]. These results have been confirmed in an independent study [13]. In spite of these data, early clinical trials targeting either EGFR or HER2 were mixed.

snippet.text:
Genomic profiling has identified ERBB2 amplification and mutations, encoding overexpressed or hyperactivated HER2, and ERBB3 (encoding HER3) alterations as drivers of human cancers (1). When ERBB2 (HER2) is amplified or mutated, it becomes activated in a ligand-independent manner, driving activation of downstream pathways controlling the migration, proliferation, survival, and differentiation of cancer cells (1). Multiple HER2targeted therapies have been approved to treat HER2 amplification and/or overexpression in breast cancer via different mechanisms of action, including monoclonal antibodies (mAb; e.g., trastuzumab), tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI, e.g., neratinib), and antibody-drug conjugates [ADC, e.g., trastuzumab emtansine and trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd); ref . 2]. 

Trastuzumab and T-DXd are also approved for the treatment of HER2amplified and/or -overexpressed gastric cancers (3). In the last 2 years, T-DXd was approved to treat non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with select ERBB2 mutations (4), and tucatinib plus trastuzumab was approved to treat HER2 amplification and/or overexpression in colorectal cancer (CRC) (5). Most recently, T-DXd received pan-tumor approval for unresectable or metastatic HER2-overexpressing (IHC 3+) solid tumors (6)(7)(8). 

Recent trials investigating HER2-targeted therapies have demonstrated efficacy in solid tumors with ERBB2 (HER2) alterations in indications which have not been approved by the U.S. FDA (9). Specifically, the lack of approved HER2-targeted therapies for non-NSCLC with ERBB2 mutations in the absence of amplification/overexpression suggests an unmet clinical need for a substantial population of patients (10,11).

documents.title: Determinants of sensitivity to HER2-targeted antibody drug conjugates in urothelial cancer
documents.snippet: HER2, encoded by the ERBB2 gene, is a receptor tyrosine kinase frequently activated in human cancers via gene amplification, mutation, and/or protein overexpression. In an analysis of 42,415 prospectively analyzed solid tumors, we show that 14.5% of urothelial cancers (n = 295/2,035) have oncogenic or likely oncogenic ERBB2 alterations (6.7% ERBB2 mutation, 6.3% amplification of wildtype ERBB2, and 1.5% concurrent mutation and amplification). Discordance of ERBB2 mutational status between primary and metastatic disease sites is common in patients with urothelial cancer as is discordance of ERBB2 mutational status between patient-derived organoid/xenograft models and the tumors from which they were derived. In patient-derived urothelial cancer models, the HER2-targeted antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) trastuzumab deruxtecan is significantly more effective than the HER kinase inhibitor neratinib. In a real-world cohort of patients with urothelial cancer treated with trastuzumab deruxtecan, co-mutation and amplification of ERBB2 is associated with exceptional clinical response. Our data support expanded clinical trials of HER2-targeted ADCs for urothelial cancers with low HER2 expression, the clinical testing of HER2 ADCs with alternative cytotoxic payloads, and the development of functional precision oncology platforms capable of assessing payload sensitivity pre-treatment as a guide to individualized therapy selection. Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) is a HER2-targeted antibody drug conjugate. Through integrated laboratory and clinical studies, the authors identify significant ERBB2 (the gene that encodes the HER2 protein) mutational heterogeneity in patients with urothelial cancer and co-mutation and amplification of ERBB2 as a potential biomarker of exceptional response to T-DXd.

attempts.answer:
Summary answer
Bladder cancer’s current early detection and precision medicine ecosystem reflects a reciprocal co-evolution: long-standing clinical challenges (high recurrence, invasive and insensitive surveillance) drove development of molecular urine assays and risk models, while integrative genomic and epigenomic landscape mapping (from early candidate genes through TCGA-scale profiling) provided the mechanistic and biomarker foundations that enabled precision diagnostics and targeted therapies. In other words, both forces were essential—clinical observations set the problem and prioritized actionable endpoints, and genetic/epigenetic discoveries supplied the measurable alterations and pathways that could be operationalized into tests and treatments. <cite id="d97e7354-0">Diagnostic workup has long combined urinalysis, cytology, cystoscopy, and imaging because cystoscopy is burdensome and cytology has low sensitivity (30–40%), motivating more effective early detection and surveillance</cite>. <cite id="cad37194-2">Systematic molecular profiling—from candidate-gene approaches and comparative genomic hybridization to next-generation sequencing programs such as TCGA—mapped frequent alterations (e.g., HRAS, TP53, RB1, FGFR3, PIK3CA), copy-number changes, and methylation patterns across urothelial carcinoma</cite>. <cite id="d8513df7-1">FGFR3 alterations emerged as potent oncogenic drivers present in about half of tumors, with mutually exclusive relationships to TP53/RB1 aberrations and predictive value for response to FGFR inhibitors, linking landscape features to both detection and therapy</cite>.

1) Clinical observations set the problem and prioritized biomarker development
For decades, clinicians faced recurrent disease and uncertain risk in non–muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC), with cystoscopy being the gold standard but limited by cost, discomfort, sampling error, and understaging, and urine cytology often insensitive (about 14–40% sensitivity overall; higher in high grade). These constraints created a clear unmet need for noninvasive, sensitive, and specific biomarkers that could guide surveillance and treatment intensity. <cite id="d97e7354-0">Cytology alone showed 14% sensitivity at 100% specificity in detection cohorts, underscoring its limitations in routine practice</cite>. <cite id="d97e7354-2">Urine cytology remains a specific adjunct to cystoscopy, yet the ideal marker has not been identified, reflecting persistent clinical gaps</cite>. <cite id="d97e7354-3">NMIBC recurs in up to 70% and progression is common, but TURBT under-stages up to 50%, reinforcing the need for reliable noninvasive biomarkers to improve diagnostic accuracy and personalize care</cite>. <cite id="d97e7354-1">Narrative syntheses from 2005–2025 emphasize that diagnostic innovations, risk stratification, and liquid biopsy are shifting paradigms toward precision-based, multimodal approaches in NMIBC</cite>. These clinical imperatives directly shaped which alterations were prioritized for molecular development (e.g., actionable driver mutations in low-grade Ta disease like FGFR3 and PIK3CA), because they aligned with the phenotype of frequent low-grade, noninvasive tumors and the surveillance challenge.

2) Landscape mapping milestones: from candidate genes to integrative genomics
Early molecular studies identified recurrent point mutations and chromosomal aberrations in bladder cancer, establishing a framework for disease mechanisms and subtypes. <cite id="cad37194-2">Candidate oncogenes such as HRAS, TP53, RB1, TSC1, FGFR3, and PIK3CA were discovered early on; comparative genomic hybridization revealed recurrent amplicons (e.g., PPARG, E2F3, EGFR, CCND1, MDM2) and losses (CDKN2A, RB1)</cite>. The TCGA integrated genomic program crystallized the landscape by coupling mutations, copy-number changes, RNA/microRNA expression, CpG methylation, and proteomics in 131 muscle-invasive tumors, defining recurrent driver modules and mutational signatures (e.g., APOBEC enrichment) that stratify biology. <cite id="cad37194-2">TCGA’s comprehensive analysis mapped mutation rates/frequencies, deletions/amplifications, expression changes, and methylation, providing a systems-level blueprint for urothelial carcinoma</cite>. <cite id="cad37194-3">Molecular profiling syntheses report that NMIBC is characterized by frequent FGFR3 and PIK3CA mutations, loss of chromosome 9, and widespread chromatin-remodeling gene alterations, whereas MIBC shows high genomic instability with recurrent TP53, RB1, and chromatin modifier mutations; transcriptomic classes (luminal, basal/squamous, stroma-rich, neuroendocrine-like) have distinct behaviors</cite>. <cite id="cad37194-1">Within TCGA data, FGFR3 emerged as a main differentially mutated gene, with inverse correlation to progression stage and protective associations, linking genomics to clinical course</cite>. These discoveries provided the mechanistic rationale and measurable targets that could be translated into diagnostic assays and therapies.

3) How landscape discoveries enabled modern early detection
Two complementary lines of translation emerged: mutation-based urine panels and methylation-based classifiers, both leveraging TCGA-defined recurrent alterations. <cite id="d8513df7-4">Combining urinary FGFR3 mutation status with promoter hypermethylation of HS3ST2, SEPTIN9, and SLIT2 achieved 97.6%/84.8% sensitivity/specificity for diagnosis (AUC ~0.96) and improved surveillance performance, illustrating how actionable driver and epigenetic markers from the landscape can be integrated into urine assays</cite>. <cite id="d97e7354-0">A sequencing-based hybrid capture assay (uCAP-Seq) targeting >450 genes demonstrated in detection cohorts 83% sensitivity at 97% specificity in a tumor-naive, predominantly pTa/low-grade setting, far outperforming cytology (14% sensitivity), explicitly using TCGA-derived knowledge of common driver regions to design the panel</cite>. <cite id="d8513df7-0">Urine panels that assay multiple genomic/epigenomic markers achieve high sensitivity and specificity for detection, and can be adapted to detect FGFR3 fusions and variants across tissue and urine, supporting feasibility for companion diagnostics</cite>. <cite id="d8513df7-3">FGFR3 mutation detection in urine sediments predicts disease presence and recurrence and associates with longer survival, supporting its use as a prognostic and surveillance biomarker</cite>. <cite id="d97e7354-4">Urine tumor DNA multidimensional predictors using UC-specific mutations and large copy-number variations detected urothelial carcinoma with 92.8% specificity and improved sensitivity versus cytology and FISH for minimal residual disease, exemplifying how DNA alterations and CNVs from the landscape can be operationalized in noninvasive tests</cite>. These assays were enabled by the prior mapping that established which alterations are recurrent, actionable, and informative for prognosis, and they were designed to meet clinical endpoints (sensitivity, specificity, NPV) that clinicians had long sought in surveillance.

4) From landscape to precision medicine: biomarker-driven therapy
Multiple precision oncology directions have been catalyzed by landscape discoveries:
- FGFR pathway addiction: <cite id="d8513df7-1">FGFR3 genomic alterations are potent oncogenic drivers and predictive biomarkers of response to FGFR inhibitors; they occur in roughly half of bladder cancers and are mutually exclusive with TP53/RB1 alterations, defining a distinct molecular subset</cite>. <cite id="d8513df7-0">Urine-based detection of FGFR3 variants and fusions is technically feasible and tissue-urine concordant, supporting use as companion/selective diagnostics in focal biomarker-driven therapy</cite>.
- HRD/RTK-addicted strategies: <cite id="cad37194-3">NMIBC is enriched for FGFR3 and PIK3CA mutations and chromatin-remodeling gene alterations; MIBC harbors recurrent TP53/RB1/chromatin modifier aberrations and RTK/RAS/PI3K pathway activity, indicating actionable classes that can guide therapy selection</cite>. Clinical development has leveraged these genomic patterns to deploy targeted agents and adaptive surveillance, with trials in RTK-fusion or HRD-positive disease informing companion diagnostic design.
- Epigenetic stratification for surveillance: <cite id="d8513df7-4">Promoter hypermethylation markers (HS3ST2/SEPTIN9/SLIT2) combined with FGFR3 mutation status both diagnose and predict recurrence, enabling risk-adapted follow-up and therapy</cite>.
- Liquid biopsy to personalize systemic therapy: <cite id="d97e7354-3">Urine-based liquid biopsy detects tumor-derived DNA and genomic alterations with improved sensitivity over cytology, supporting noninvasive response assessment and MRD monitoring in early-stage disease; imaging complements these noninvasive modalities</cite>. 
Importantly, some biomarkers have matured into clinical approval and practice-changing algorithms (e.g., FGFR3-targeted agents; HRD-guided PARP inhibition in trials), while others (e.g., comprehensive HRD panels) are still being validated for clinical utility; this heterogeneity reflects the uneven translation of epigenomic and genomic profiles into robust, patient-level decision tools.

5) Synthesis: a reciprocal co-evolution, not an either/or
The evidence indicates a feedback loop rather than a strict linear sequence: clinical observations (recurrent NMIBC, limited cytology, need for risk-adapted care) defined priorities and endpoints, while landscape mapping (candidate genes, CGH, TCGA-scale integration) provided the measurable alterations and pathways to meet those needs. <cite id="d97e7354-0">Because cytology sensitivity is often low and cystoscopy is burdensome, liquid biopsy approaches built on TCGA-derived panels achieved substantially higher sensitivity/specificity and are being integrated into detection and surveillance algorithms</cite>. <cite id="d97e7354-2">Reviews emphasize the need for additional biological insight into progression and the importance of investigating the genetic and epigenetic changes that drive disease, linking discovery to clinical impact</cite>. <cite id="d8513df7-1">FGFR3-focused reviews show how oncogenic pathway delineation and clinical-genomic correlations enabled predictive biomarker-guided therapy and a companion diagnostic ecosystem</cite>. <cite id="cad37194-2">Integrative programs such as TCGA transformed understanding by jointly quantifying mutations, CNAs, and methylation, creating the substrate for diagnostic classifiers and therapeutic hypotheses</cite>. 

Boundary conditions and open questions
- Scope of clinical utility: <cite id="d97e7354-1">While personalized surveillance using circulating/urine tumor DNA is promising and may reduce procedural burden, large-scale validation and real-world data are still required to establish widespread clinical utility</cite>. <cite id="d97e7354-4">Noninvasive urine DNA assays can match or exceed cytology and FISH for MRD, but their role in initial diagnosis and across diverse-stage populations continues to mature</cite>.
- HRD and immune-oncology: <cite id="cad37194-3">Genomic instability, TP53/RB1 alterations, and APOBEC signatures are prominent in muscle-invasive disease, guiding immunotherapy and chemotherapy contexts, but the translation of HRD-associated epigenetic profiles into routine, reproducible clinical decision rules remains an active area of development</cite>.
- Clinical first vs discovery first: <cite id="d97e7354-0">Many current assays explicitly “assay regions known to harbor common driver mutations” from TCGA, illustrating that discovery preceded and enabled assay design</cite>, while <cite id="d97e7354-3">the persistent limitations of cytology and the burden of cystoscopy drove the prioritization of noninvasive molecular approaches</cite>. Together, they produced a modern paradigm where discovery defines targets and clinical need shapes deployment and endpoints.

Bottom line
- The genetic and epigenetic landscape of bladder cancer was discovered and systemically mapped through integrative genomics, providing actionable targets and risk-stratifying features that directly enabled improved early detection and precision therapy frameworks. <cite id="d97e7354-0">Urine assays leveraging TCGA-derived driver regions outperformed cytology in sensitivity while maintaining high specificity, enabling adoption in detection and surveillance</cite>; <cite id="d8513df7-1">FGFR3 alterations’ oncogenic and predictive biology enabled targeted therapies with companion diagnostics</cite>; <cite id="cad37194-2">TCGA-scale programs codified the recurrent mutations, CNAs, and methylation patterns underpinning these applications</cite>.
- At the same time, longstanding clinical observations—burden and recurrence, poor cytology—driven the identification and prioritization of actionable alterations (e.g., FGFR3 in low-grade Ta disease) and shaped the development of assays to meet clinical endpoints. <cite id="d97e7354-0">Cytology’s low sensitivity catalyzed high-sensitivity liquid biopsy approaches</cite>; <cite id="d8513df7-3">FGFR3 mutation served as an early driver concept validated clinically for prognosis and surveillance</cite>.
- Therefore, both forces were necessary: clinical observations framed the problem and selected targets for translational validation, while genetic/epigenetic discoveries provided the measurable, clinically actionable landscape that enabled today’s early detection and precision medicine practices. <cite id="d97e7354-1">Contemporary guidance anticipates further convergence of molecular biomarkers, immunotherapy, and novel delivery systems into precision, multimodal NMIBC management</cite>.

Title: Development of an extended version of GALEAS bladder: Detection of FGFR3 fusions in urine and associations between genomic alterations and gene expression

Title: Role of FGFR3 in bladder cancer: Treatment landscape and future challenges.
Snippet: Bladder cancer is a heterogeneous malignancy and is responsible for approximately 3.2% of new diagnoses of cancer per year (Sung et al., 2021). Fibroblast Growth Factor Receptors (FGFRs) have recently emerged as a novel therapeutic target in cancer. In particular, FGFR3 genomic alterations are potent oncogenic drivers in bladder cancer and represent predictive biomarkers of response to FGFR inhibitors. Indeed, overall ∼50% of bladder cancers have somatic mutations in the FGFR3 -coding sequence (Cappellen et al., 1999; Turner and Grose, 2010). FGFR3 gene rearrangements are typical alterations in bladder cancer (Nelson et al., 2016; Parker et al., 2014). In this review, we summarize the most relevant evidence on the role of FGFR3 and the state-of-art of anti-FGFR3 treatment in bladder cancer. Furthermore, we interrogated the AACR Project GENIE to investigate clinical and molecular features of FGFR3-altered bladder cancers. We found that FGFR3 rearrangements and missense mutations were associated with a lower fraction of mutated genome, compared to the FGFR3 wild-type tumors, as also observed in other oncogene-addicted cancers. Moreover, we observed that FGFR3 genomic alterations are mutually exclusive with other genomic aberrations of canonical bladder cancer oncogenes, such as TP53 and RB1. Finally, we provide an overview of the treatment landscape of FGFR3-altered bladder cancer, discussing future perspectives for the management of this disease.
</snippet>

Title: Urinary Tumor DNA-Based Diagnosis and Surveillance for Nonmuscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer—Current Landscape and Future Directions

Additionally, cytology comes with significant limitations in the form of low sensitivity [8]. Previous meta-analyses have demonstrated overall sensitivities ranging from 30% to 40%, with higher-grade disease associated with greater sensitivity. Because of this, surveillance of nonmuscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) beyond cystoscopy poses great challenges.

Title: Diagnosis, evaluation, and management of patients with non-muscle invasive bladder cancer
Snippet: Abstract Introduction Non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) accounts for over 75% of bladder cancer cases worldwide and is associated with high recurrence rates and significant surveillance costs. Advances in diagnostic modalities, risk stratification, and bladder-preserving therapies have transformed management strategies. Areas Covered This narrative review synthesizes evidence from 70 key publications identified through a comprehensive search of PubMed, MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and Google Scholar (2005–2025). Topics include clinical presentation, diagnostic innovations such as enhanced cystoscopy and urinary biomarkers, contemporary risk stratification models, and evolving treatment paradigms including intravesical therapy, immunotherapy, and gene therapy. 
Expert Opinion/Commentary
 NMIBC management is shifting toward precision-based, multimodal approaches that integrate molecular biomarkers, immunotherapy, and novel drug delivery systems. While early-phase trials show promise, large-scale studies and real-world data are essential to validate these strategies. Personalized surveillance using circulating and urinary tumor DNA may reduce procedural burden and improve outcomes, marking a paradigm shift toward adaptive, patient-centered care.

Snippet: Bladder cancer remains a common malignancy in Western society, with global incidence of over 356,000 new cases per year (Ploeg et al., 2009). In non-muscle-invasive tumors, recurrence and progression to muscle-invasive disease are the critical steps that dictate therapy and are associated with worse survival rates. Title: Diagnostic and Prognostic Non-Invasive Markers in Bladder Cancer
Snippet: Bladder cancer is one of the most common malignancies worldwide, with more than 614,000 new cases diagnosed annually [1]. It is characterized by a high rate of recurrence, particularly in non-muscle-invasive disease, where recurrence occurs in up to 70% of patients during follow-up [2,3]. The global burden of bladder cancer is projected to increase substantially, with its annual incidence and mortality estimated to rise by 73% and 87%, respectively, by 2040, underscoring the urgent need for improved diagnostic and therapeutic strategies [4]. Urothelial carcinoma accounts for approximately 90-95% of all cases of bladder cancer [5,6]. Bladder cancer is broadly classified into non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) and muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC). The presence or absence of detrusor muscle invasion is the pivotal landmark that distinguishes these two types, because this landmark dictates the transition from bladder-preserving strategies to more aggressive definitive treatments [2,7]. These fundamentally different prognostic and therapeutic implications underscore the clinical necessity for accurate T-staging [6,8]. Cystoscopy and transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) remain the gold standard for diagnosis and staging. However, TURBT is associated with notable limitations, including sampling error and understaging in up to 50% of cases [9][10][11][12], underscoring the need for reliable, non-invasive biomarkers that can improve diagnostic accuracy and guide clinical decision-making. 

Recent advances in molecular diagnostics have expanded the landscape of noninvasive biomarkers, particularly through urine-based liquid-biopsy approaches that enable the detection of tumor-derived DNA and genomic alterations with encouraging diagnostic performance [13]. These molecular assays, including mutation-based panels targeting genes such as TERT, FGFR3, and PIK3CA, have demonstrated improved sensitivity compared with conventional urine cytology, although their role in clinical practice continues to develop [13][14][15][16]. 

In addition to molecular and urine-based approaches, imaging has emerged as a distinct and increasingly important category of non-invasive biomarkers in bladder cancer.
</snippet>

Title: Letter to the Editor: clinical utility of urine DNA for noninvasive detection and minimal residual disease monitoring in urothelial carcinoma
Snippet: Current methods for the early detection and minimal residual disease (MRD) monitoring of urothelial carcinoma (UC) are invasive and/or possess suboptimal sensitivity. We developed an efficient workflow named urine tumor DNA multidimensional bioinformatic predictor (utLIFE). Using UC-specific mutations and large copy number variations, the utLIFE-UC model was developed on a bladder cancer cohort ( n  = 150) and validated in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) bladder cancer cohort ( n  = 674) and an upper tract urothelial carcinoma (UTUC) cohort ( n  = 22). The utLIFE-UC model could discriminate 92.8% of UCs with 96.0% specificity and was robustly validated in the BLCA_TCGA and UTUC cohorts. Furthermore, compared to cytology, utLIFE-UC improved the sensitivity of bladder cancer detection ( p  < 0.01). In the MRD cohort, utLIFE-UC could distinguish 100% of patients with residual disease, showing superior sensitivity compared to cytology ( p  < 0.01) and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH, p  < 0.05). This study shows that utLIFE-UC can be used to detect UC with high sensitivity and specificity in patients with early-stage cancer or MRD. The utLIFE-UC is a cost-effective, rapid, high-throughput, noninvasive, and promising approach that may reduce the burden of cystoscopy and blind surgery.
</snippet></tool_output>
