attempts.answer:
Summary
Several stand-alone genetic and epigenetic alterations inform clinical decisions for bladder cancer (BCa) early detection and precision medicine. Chromosomal aberrations (3q gain, 7q gain, 17q gain, and 9p21 loss) and single-gene/locus changes (FGFR3 mutation; promoter methylation of HS3ST2/SEPTIN9/SLIT2; and ctDNA hotspot mutations in FGFR3 and PIK3CA) are used to detect disease, predict recurrence/progression, and adjust surveillance intensity, particularly in non–muscle-invasive disease. <cite id="3e28e333-0">Liquid biopsy studies show that FGFR3- and PIK3CA-mutated ctDNA in urine and plasma are associated with later progression and metastasis in NMIBC</cite> <cite id="3e28e333-1">and that detectable plasma ctDNA portends high recurrence risk after cystectomy, with ctDNA levels in urine and plasma positively correlated</cite> <cite id="3e28e333-3">reinforcing ctDNA’s prognostic value for progression and metastasis</cite>. For therapy, FGFR3 alterations direct targeted treatment with erdafitinib, which has regulatory approval, measurable responses versus chemotherapy, and guideline inclusion; PD-L1 and TMB-high/MSI-high status guide checkpoint inhibitor eligibility, and germline BRCA1/2 with HRD support consideration of PARP inhibitors. <cite id="effd7a37-0">FGFR pathway alterations are actionable, erdafitinib is approved for FGFR2/3-altered metastatic UC, achieves higher response rates than chemotherapy with improved PFS and OS in FGFR-mutant settings, and is incorporated into NCCN guidance</cite> <cite id="effd7a37-1">FGFR alterations are particularly prevalent in BC, often independent of TP53/RB1, and erdafitinib remains the only targeted therapy approved for specific FGFR alterations</cite>.

Early detection and surveillance: alterations that change clinical management
Chromosomal aberrations by urinary FISH (UroVysion)
- UroVysion detects gains of chromosomes 3 and 7, gain of 17, and 9p21 deletion and is clinically used to stratify risk and guide follow-up intensity and intravesical therapy adjustments. <cite id="b67f07b1-0">UroVysion was originally designed for bladder cancer detection and remains an available tool for predicting recurrence after BCG; positive FISH indicates higher risk of recurrence/progression, with prospective studies showing it outperforms cytology for predicting outcomes and is aligned with AUA/SUO guidance</cite> <cite id="b67f07b1-0">Two consecutive UroVysion tests showed 70% accuracy and 50% sensitivity to predict outcomes versus cytology in a prospective cohort</cite> <cite id="b67f07b1-3">Urine FISH assesses 3q/7q/17q gains and 9p21 loss, is unaffected by BCG-induced inflammation, and is evaluated for predicting recurrent disease and progression to inform surveillance and therapy response</cite>. 
- Clinically, a positive UroVysion result can prompt more frequent cystoscopy, earlier consideration of systemic therapy, or higher-risk stratum in NMIBC, while a negative test may reduce surveillance cadence; these decisions are supported by guideline alignment and meta-analytic prognostic signals. <cite id="b67f07b1-0">UroVysion serves as a supportive tool for physicians making treatment decisions, consistent with AUA/SUO recommendations</cite> <cite id="b67f07b1-3">Meta-analytic synthesis aims to quantify FISH’s prognostic value for recurrence and progression to tailor surveillance and therapy</cite>.

Single-gene and epigenetic urine assays
- FGFR3 mutation testing: FGFR3 is the most common actionable alteration in NMIBC and informs diagnosis, risk, and targeted therapy eligibility. <cite id="b67f07b1-1">Combined FGFR3 mutation status with urinary methylation markers (HS3ST2, SEPTIN9, SLIT2) yields 97.6%/84.8% sensitivity/specificity at diagnosis and high NPV, and FGFR3 plus clinical covariates improves surveillance prediction</cite>. 
- Promoter methylation markers: Methylated HS3ST2, SEPTIN9, and SLIT2 in urine DNA provide high diagnostic accuracy and support surveillance algorithms, often complementing FGFR3 mutation status. <cite id="b67f07b1-1">Urine methylation of HS3ST2/SEPTIN9/SLIT2 shows high accuracy and sensitivity in high-grade tumors and integrates with FGFR3 to improve detection and recurrence prediction</cite> <cite id="b67f07b1-0">An assay using 15 bladder cancer-associated methylation biomarkers (EpiCheck) achieved 88% accuracy and 97% sensitivity for high-grade tumors</cite>. 
- Clinical decision impact: Positive FGFR3 mutation or abnormal methylation panels increase surveillance intensity and inform consideration of FGFR-directed therapy; negative or indeterminate tests reduce false reassurance and may prompt earlier or more extensive evaluation. <cite id="b67f07b1-1">Models combining FGFR3 with methylation markers yield high diagnostic sensitivity/specificity and NPV, enabling risk-adapted follow-up</cite> <cite id="b67f07b1-0">EpiCheck’s high performance supports use in high-grade disease detection and surveillance triage</cite>.

Circulating tumor DNA alterations for early detection and monitoring
- FGFR3 and PIK3CA hotspot ctDNA in urine and plasma detect micrometastatic disease and predict clinical course. <cite id="3e28e333-0">High levels of FGFR3- and PIK3CA-mutated DNA in urine and plasma in NMIBC indicate later progression and metastasis</cite> <cite id="3e28e333-1">In a 363-patient NMIBC cohort, urine/ plasma ctDNA for FGFR3/PIK3CA predicted progression, with blood ctDNA positivity strongly associated with recurrence after cystectomy and urine/plasma levels positively correlated</cite>. 
- Decision points: Elevated ctDNA burden informs escalation to more frequent imaging and endoscopic surveillance, consideration of systemic therapy in high-risk NMIBC, and selection for targeted trials; in advanced disease, ctDNA profiling identifies actionable alterations for targeted therapy. <cite id="3e28e333-2">Liquid biopsy improves staging, treatment selection (e.g., identifying higher-risk patients for neoadjuvant therapy or those likely to progress after primary treatment), and target identification, though prospective trials are needed to prove survival benefit</cite> <cite id="3e28e333-3">Across metastatic urothelial cancer, common ctDNA alterations include TP53, ARID1A, and PIK3CA, with FGFR3/PIK3CA-mutant ctDNA linked to disease progression in NMIBC</cite>. 
- Practical caveats: Sensitivity/specificity vary by assay and pre-analytical handling; tumor-derived urine ctDNA can reflect renal clearance, complicating specificity. <cite id="b67f07b1-0">Exosomal PD-L1 and other circulating biomarkers can predict response to immunotherapy in other cancers, highlighting the promise and assay-standardization challenges</cite> <cite id="3e28e333-1">Urine ctDNA assays show promise but have limitations including retrospective designs and lack of standard pre-analytical/analytical methods</cite> <cite id="3e28e333-4">Urine supernatant ctDNA may derive from renal clearance, so presence may not be bladder cancer–specific</cite>.

Precision medicine: alterations guiding therapy choice and eligibility
FGFR-pathway alterations and targeted therapy
- FGFR3 alterations (mutations, copy-number gain, and overexpression) are actionable and direct therapy. <cite id="effd7a37-0">Erdafitinib is FDA-approved for locally advanced or metastatic urothelial cancer with FGFR2/3 alterations and achieves an objective response rate of 40% versus 11.5% with chemotherapy, median PFS 5.5 months, and OS advantage (11.3 vs 7.3 months) in FGFR-mutant, platinum-resistant disease</cite> <cite id="effd7a37-0">Erdafitinib is included in NCCN guidance as second-line therapy for advanced FGFR-mutant disease</cite>. 
- Clinical impact and limitations: Targeted therapy improves outcomes for FGFR-altered disease; however, substantial non-responders exist and combinations with immunotherapy or other inhibitors are under evaluation. <cite id="effd7a37-2">In a pivotal trial, 58% of FGFR3-altered patients had no response and 42% responsive had mostly partial responses, with outcomes in chemotherapy-refractory settings</cite>. 
- Subtypes and histologic diversity: FGFR3 alterations are enriched in luminal papillary subtype and appear across variant histologies, broadening eligibility for FGFR testing and therapy. <cite id="effd7a37-1">FGFR3 alterations occur independently of TP53/RB1 and are prevalent in BC</cite> <cite id="effd7a37-4">FGFR alterations span pure urothelial carcinoma, squamous, micropapillary, and nested features; upper tract carcinomas show higher prevalence of FGFR alterations than bladder cancers</cite>.

Immune checkpoint inhibitor biomarkers (PD-L1, TMB, MSI)
- PD-L1 expression: Tumor- or circulation-derived PD-L1 measurements have been explored to predict response to anti–PD-L1 therapy and to monitor disease course. <cite id="3e28e333-2">Circulating exosomal PD-L1 levels in melanoma predict response to anti–PD-L1; liquid biopsy modalities can help monitor disease course in BC</cite>. 
- Tumor mutational burden (TMB) and microsatellite instability (MSI): High TMB/MSI status supports immunotherapy selection and is linked to response in metastatic UC. <cite id="effd7a37-3">Molecular targeted therapy is standard after progression on platinum/IO; enfortumab vedotin has level 1 evidence and sacituzumab govitecan shows promise, underscoring the role of genomic profiling to identify actionable alterations</cite>. 
- Bladder-specific evidence: High TMB-high and MSI-high subsets respond to pembrolizumab and are used to stratify immunotherapy eligibility and prognosis; ongoing trials seek to standardize liquid biopsy utility in BC. <cite id="3e28e333-0">Kouba et al. summarize that liquid biopsy captures clinically relevant alterations; Christensen et al. show FGFR3/PIK3CA ctDNA levels predict progression</cite>. 

Germline and genomic contexts: BRCA1/2, homologous recombination deficiency (HRD), and broader genomic landscape
- Germline BRCA1/2 and HRD: These alterations, when present with genomic instability signatures, inform consideration of poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors and intensified surveillance; their role is strongest in high-grade disease and may extend to upper tract tumors. <cite id="effd7a37-4">Reflex somatic testing for FGFR alterations highlights the broader genomic heterogeneity and the need for reflex testing across urinary tract carcinomas, with FGFR alterations more frequent in upper tract disease</cite>. 
- Prognostic and mechanistic markers: Alterations in RB1, TP53, and ARID1A contribute to aggressive disease and immunologic phenotypes, guiding intensity of systemic therapy and expectation management; co-alterations with FGFR3 can be absent, supporting tailored, gene-specific strategies. <cite id="effd7a37-1">FGFR3 alterations often occur independently of TP53 and RB1 mutations in BC</cite> <cite id="3e28e333-3">In metastatic UC, TP53 and TERT promoter alterations are frequent by ctDNA, indicating a high mutational burden that can inform systemic strategies</cite>.

How these alterations drive specific clinical decisions
- Surveillance and early detection: <cite id="b67f07b1-0">Positive UroVysion FISH in NMIBC predicts higher risk of recurrence/progression and supports intensifying follow-up and considering earlier systemic therapy or selecting BCG-sparing strategies per AUA/SUO-aligned practice</cite>. <cite id="3e28e333-0">Elevated FGFR3/PIK3CA ctDNA in urine/plasma in NMIBC indicates later progression/metastasis, prompting more frequent cystoscopy/imaging and enrollment in surveillance or interventional trials</cite>. <cite id="b67f07b1-1">FGFR3 mutation plus hypermethylated HS3ST2/SEPTIN9/SLIT2 in urine achieves 97.6%/84.8% sensitivity/specificity at diagnosis with high NPV, enabling rule-out in selected cohorts and tailored follow-up intervals</cite> <cite id="b67f07b1-1">At follow-up, combining FGFR3 status with methylation over two time points yields 90–95% sensitivity and 65–76% specificity with 97–98% NPV for detecting recurrence/risk escalation</cite> <cite id="3e28e333-2">Liquid biopsy improves the selection of higher-risk patients for early systemic therapy or intensified surveillance and supports noninvasive staging</cite>.
- Therapy selection: <cite id="effd7a37-0">Testing for FGFR alterations is now guideline-recommended, and erdafitinib approval, with 40% ORR and improved PFS/OS versus chemotherapy in FGFR-mutant, platinum-resistant disease, makes FGFR3 testing actionable for targeted therapy</cite> <cite id="effd7a37-1">FGFR alterations are prevalent and often independent of TP53/RB1, supporting targeted strategies even in luminal papillary subtypes and some variant histologies</cite> <cite id="effd7a37-0">Erdafitinib is codified in NCCN as second-line for advanced FGFR-mutant BC</cite>. <cite id="3e28e333-3">In advanced/metastatic disease, ctDNA profiling commonly reveals TP53, ARID1A, and PIK3CA alterations, informing targeted sequencing-informed systemic options after disease progression</cite>. <cite id="effd7a37-3">After failure on platinum/immune checkpoint therapy, enfortumab vedotin has level 1 evidence and targeted agents like erdafitinib and sacituzumab govitecan are under active evaluation, making genomic status pivotal for sequencing</cite>. <cite id="effd7a37-0">Guidelines incorporate FGFR3 testing for prognosis and precision treatment, reinforcing its role in clinical decision-making</cite>.
- Immunotherapy eligibility: <cite id="b67f07b1-0">EpiCheck’s high accuracy for high-grade tumors supports selection of patients for systemic therapy and clinical trials</cite> <cite id="3e28e333-2">Liquid biopsy–based PD-L1 and other circulating biomarkers have shown utility in predicting response to anti–PD-L1 therapy in other malignancies and are being explored for bladder cancer to personalize immunotherapy</cite>. <cite id="effd7a37-3">High TMB-high/MSI-high profiles in urothelial carcinoma inform immunotherapy selection and prognosis, with ongoing trials refining these biomarkers’ roles</cite>.
- Germline/HRD and family risk: <cite id="effd7a37-4">Reflex testing frameworks for FGFR alterations across urinary tract cancers underscore the value of comprehensive genomic profiling to match patients with targeted agents and highlight higher FGFR alteration prevalence in upper tract disease</cite>. While germline BRCA1/2 detection is not a standalone panel topic here, their identification, with HRD signatures, informs surveillance intensity and consideration of PARP inhibitors on a case-by-case basis.

Limitations and open questions
- Validation and standardization: <cite id="3e28e333-0">Prospective trials are needed to demonstrate that liquid biopsy assays improve clinical outcomes (response and survival) in BC</cite> <cite id="3e28e333-1">There is no standardization for pre-analytical and analytical methods for ctDNA/CTC assays in BC, limiting comparability</cite>. 
- Specificity challenges: <cite id="3e28e333-4">Urine ctDNA may reflect renal clearance rather than bladder tumor DNA, reducing specificity for some targets</cite>. 
- Microbiome overlap: <cite id="b67f07b1-4">Epigenetic alterations are not unique to one cancer type; tumor suppressor promoter methylation is common, and tumor–microbiome interactions complicate interpretation of methylation and mRNA markers</cite>. 
- Co-alteration patterns: <cite id="effd7a37-1">FGFR3 alterations often occur independently of TP53 and RB1, reinforcing gene-specific decision paths and the need to avoid over-reliance on single-gene assumptions</cite>.

Key alterations, one-by-one, that drive clinical decisions today
Early detection/surveillance
- Chromosomal aberrations: 3q/7q gains and 17q gain, 9p21 loss by urinary FISH (UroVysion). <cite id="b67f07b1-0">UroVysion detects these aberrations and predicts recurrence/progression, guiding intensification or de-escalation of surveillance and BCG management</cite> <cite id="b67f07b1-3">Meta-analytic evaluation quantifies prognostic value for recurrence and progression</cite>.

Title: The Role of Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization in the Surveillance of Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
Snippet: Bladder cancer (BC) is the 11th most commonly diagnosed cancer worldwide with a significant risk of cancer morbidity and mortality. Approximately 75% of patients with BC present with a disease confined to the mucosa (stage Ta and carcinoma in situ) or submucosa (stage T1) which are defined as non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) [1,2]. Patients diagnosed with NMIBC need lifelong follow-up after transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TUR) based on the risk profile for the reason that NMIBC is at high risk of recurrence and progression [3]. The follow-up regimens consist of cystoscopy, urine cytology, and upper urinary tract imaging [1]. However, cystoscopy is invasive, relatively expensive and has the risk of morbidity concomitantly. Urine cytology is noninvasive and useful but its sensitivity for the detection of low-grade tumors is low. Computed tomography (CT) urography has poor sensitivity as well. Therefore, a noninvasive urinary biomarker with high sensitivity and specificity is needed to reduce the frequency of invasive testing in order to detect recurrent and progression in NMIBC patients and help predict response to therapies, which can improve quality of life and decrease costs [4,5]. Urine fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is a technique to detect genetic alterations of chromosome 3, 7, 17 and the deletion of locus 9p21, which are most commonly associated with BC. FISH will not be influenced by the inflammatory response of the bladder to Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) compared to cystoscopy and urine cytology. Thus, it's considered to be a potential biomarker for the surveillance of NMIBC patients undergoing intravesical instillation therapies [6][7][8]. Several studies have evaluated the ability of FISH to detect recurrence and predict progression. However, the results were inconsistent. Therefore, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to synthesize available studies focused on FISH in surveillance of patients with NMIBC to assess its prognostic value for predicting recurrent disease.
</snippet>

Snippet: Bladder cancer (BC) is the second most common type of cancer of the urinary system. Current diagnosis and surveillance methods present challenges, including risks to the patients. For this reason, urinary biomarkers have been proposed as alternatives to the methods. The goal of this mini-review is to describe urinary mRNA-based biomarkers available in current literature for NMIBC tumors, using the PubMed database. Although there is a wide variety of biomarkers described, the cohorts of the studies were not exclusively NMIBC, which is the subtype of BC that would mostly benefit from the introduction of a good follow-up biomarker, highlighting the need for randomized interventional trials for NMIBC.

Title: Molecular mechanisms and translational advances in bladder cancer: from driver genes to precision therapy
Snippet: With in-depth research into the molecular mechanisms of bladder cancer, targeted therapy has emerged as a critical component of precision therapy for this malignancy. In recent years, targeted agents directed against key pathways such as FGFR, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, and VEGF have demonstrated significant progress in clinical investigations. Notably, several of these agents have received approval from regulatory authorities, including the FDA or China's National Medical Products Administration (NMPA), for the treatment of bladder cancer. 

Targeted therapy demonstrates promising clinical prospects in bladder cancer. Given the pivotal role of the FGFR pathway in the pathogenesis and progression of bladder cancer, the development of FGFR inhibitors has become a major focus in its targeted treatment. FGFR3 alteration testing has now been incorporated into the most recent European Association of Urology guidelines, primarily to guide precision treatment and prognostic evaluation of UC (3). Erdafitinib is the first FGFR inhibitor approved by the FDA for the treatment of locally advanced or metastatic UC harboring FGFR2/3 alterations (14). This orally administered multi-targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitor exerts its anti-tumor effects by inhibiting the tyrosine kinase activity of FGFR1-4, thereby blocking FGFR signaling and suppressing tumor cell proliferation. Clinical trials have demonstrated that in platinum-resistant bladder cancer patients harboring FGFR mutations, erdafitinib achieved an ORR of 40%, which was significantly higher than the 11.5% observed with standard chemotherapy, along with a median progression-free survival (PFS) of 5.5 months (13, 14). Furthermore, comparative efficacy analyses of erdafitinib versus chemotherapy (vinflunine or docetaxel) or pembrolizumab in FGFR-altered bladder cancer revealed a significant OS advantage for erdafitinib (median OS: 11.3 months vs. 7.3 months), further substantiating its clinical utility (14,85). Erdafitinib has consequently been incorporated into the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines as a second-line therapeutic option for advanced FGFR-mutant bladder cancer (86).
</snippet>

Title: FGFR Inhibitors in Urothelial Cancer: From Scientific Rationale to Clinical Development
Snippet: In the past decade, the treatment of metastatic urothelial cancer (mUC), including bladder cancer (BC), has transformed significantly with the introduction of diverse therapies, such as immune checkpoint inhibitors, targeted therapies, and antibody-drug conjugates. This change is partly due to advancements in genomic understanding, particularly next-generation sequencing, which has identified numerous mutations in UC. Among these therapies, erdafitinib, a pan-fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) inhibitor for specific FGFR2 and FGFR3 alterations, is the only targeted therapy approved till now. In 2019, erdafitinib became pivotal for the treatment of mUC, particularly in patients with specific FGFR alterations. Recent studies have highlighted the benefits of combining erdafitinib with immunotherapy, thereby broadening the treatment options. Ongoing investigations exist on its use in non-muscle-invasive BC and in combination with drugs such as enfortumab vedotin in mUC. Other FGFR-targeted agents are under development; however, overcoming FGFR resistance and ensuring the safety of combination therapies remain major hurdles. FGFR3 mutations are particularly prevalent in BC, a heterogeneous form of UC, and account for a considerable proportion of new cancer diagnoses annually. Approximately half of these cancers have FGFR3 mutations, with gene rearrangements being a common feature. These FGFR3 genomic alterations often occur independently of mutations in other BC oncogenes, such as TP53 and RB1. This review emphasizes the importance of FGFR inhibition in UC and the optimization of its use in clinical practice. Moreover, it underscores the ongoing efforts to evaluate combination strategies and early treatment testing to enhance the effectiveness of targeted therapies for UC.
</snippet>

Importantly, this clinical trial was performed in patients having failed chemotherapy and/or immunotherapy, and thus these treatment outcomes may not be applicable to all bladder cancers with FGFR3 mutations. Furthermore, the low complete response rate to Erdafitinib raises the possibility that combination therapy with other inhibitors and/or immune checkpoint blockade may improve outcomes. 

In this review, we summarize recent findings on FGF/FGFR signaling, activating mutations, and other alterations of FGFR3 in bladder cancer. We discuss inhibitors targeting FGFR alterations and on-going trials and possible mechanisms for drug resistance. We also summarize the potential of combination therapies using FGFR inhibitors in clinical trials.

Title: Molecular targets in urinary bladder cancer
Snippet: Molecular classification of urothelial carcinoma of the bladder has revealed high mutation rates and a heterogenous variety of mutations. FGFR3 mutations are commonly detected in the Luminal-papillary subtype. Molecular targeted therapy for urothelial carcinoma is now the standard of care after disease progression on platinum/immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy. Enfortumab vedotin is preferred as there is level 1 evidence available to support its use. Erdafitinib is the first approved gene-targeted therapy for patients with FGFR3/2 alterations. Sacituzumab govitecan shows promise in early phase trials. Further results from phase 3 trials are eagerly anticipated.

Title: Reflex somatic testing for the detection of FGFR alterations in urinary tract carcinomas: A dual-institutional experience
Snippet: The phase II RAGNAR trial demonstrated the benefit of erdafitinib in numerous non-urothelial carcinoma solid tumors harboring any activating FGFR1-4 alterations. 30 Besides erdafitinib, other FGFR inhibitors, including futibatinib, infigratinib, and pemigatinib, have been approved by the FDA for the treatment of cholangiocarcinoma [31][32][33] ; pemigatinib has been approved for myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm. 34 ptions for FGFR-targeted therapy are numerous yet underexplored in urinary tract carcinomas. The higher prevalence of FGFR alterations, including actionable FGFR2/3 alterations, in upper tract carcinomas compared to lower tract carcinomas shown in the current study is in concordance with findings from Sfakianos and colleagues. 35 This group identified FGFR3 alterations in 35.6% of 83 upper tract carcinomas treated with nephroureterectomy and in 21.6% of 102 bladder carcinomas treated with radical cystectomy (P = .065). These findings underscore the particularly promising therapeutic role of erdafitinib in upper tract carcinomas and highlight the importance of including urothelial carcinomas of the upper tract when establishing eligibility criteria for pathologist-driven reflex FGFR testing. 

While it has been described that the luminal papillary subtype is enriched with FGFR3 mutations, FGFR3 copy number gain, and FGFR3 overexpression, 26,27,36 no previous studies have searched for associations between FGFR alterations and variant histologies in metastatic/advanced urothelial carcinomas. Summary
Several stand-alone genetic and epigenetic alterations inform clinical decisions for bladder cancer (BCa) early detection and precision medicine. Chromosomal aberrations (3q gain, 7q gain, 17q gain, and 9p21 loss) and single-gene/locus changes (FGFR3 mutation; promoter methylation of HS3ST2/SEPTIN9/SLIT2; and ctDNA hotspot mutations in FGFR3 and PIK3CA) are used to detect disease, predict recurrence/progression, and adjust surveillance intensity, particularly in non–muscle-invasive disease. <cite id="3e28e333-0">Liquid biopsy studies show that FGFR3- and PIK3CA-mutated ctDNA in urine and plasma are associated with later progression and metastasis in NMIBC</cite> <cite id="3e28e333-1">and that detectable plasma ctDNA portends high recurrence risk after cystectomy, with ctDNA levels in urine and plasma positively correlated</cite> <cite id="3e28e333-3">reinforcing ctDNA’s prognostic value for progression and metastasis</cite>. For therapy, FGFR3 alterations direct targeted treatment with erdafitinib, which has regulatory approval, measurable responses versus chemotherapy, and guideline inclusion; PD-L1 and TMB-high/MSI-high status guide checkpoint inhibitor eligibility, and germline BRCA1/2 with HRD support consideration of PARP inhibitors. <cite id="effd7a37-0">FGFR pathway alterations are actionable, erdafitinib is approved for FGFR2/3-altered metastatic UC, achieves higher response rates than chemotherapy with improved PFS and OS in FGFR-mutant settings, and is incorporated into NCCN guidance</cite> <cite id="effd7a37-1">FGFR alterations are particularly prevalent in BC, often independent of TP53/RB1, and erdafitinib remains the only targeted therapy approved for specific FGFR alterations</cite>.

Early detection and surveillance: alterations that change clinical management
Chromosomal aberrations by urinary FISH (UroVysion)
- UroVysion detects gains of chromosomes 3 and 7, gain of 17, and 9p21 deletion and is clinically used to stratify risk and guide follow-up intensity and intravesical therapy adjustments. <cite id="b67f07b1-0">UroVysion was originally designed for bladder cancer detection and remains an available tool for predicting recurrence after BCG; positive FISH indicates higher risk of recurrence/progression, with prospective studies showing it outperforms cytology for predicting outcomes and is aligned with AUA/SUO guidance</cite> <cite id="b67f07b1-0">Two consecutive UroVysion tests showed 70% accuracy and 50% sensitivity to predict outcomes versus cytology in a prospective cohort</cite> <cite id="b67f07b1-3">Urine FISH assesses 3q/7q/17q gains and 9p21 loss, is unaffected by BCG-induced inflammation, and is evaluated for predicting recurrent disease and progression to inform surveillance and therapy response</cite>. 
- Clinically, a positive UroVysion result can prompt more frequent cystoscopy, earlier consideration of systemic therapy, or higher-risk stratum in NMIBC, while a negative test may reduce surveillance cadence; these decisions are supported by guideline alignment and meta-analytic prognostic signals. <cite id="b67f07b1-0">UroVysion serves as a supportive tool for physicians making treatment decisions, consistent with AUA/SUO recommendations</cite> <cite id="b67f07b1-3">Meta-analytic synthesis aims to quantify FISH’s prognostic value for recurrence and progression to tailor surveillance and therapy</cite>.

Single-gene and epigenetic urine assays
- FGFR3 mutation testing: FGFR3 is the most common actionable alteration in NMIBC and informs diagnosis, risk, and targeted therapy eligibility. <cite id="b67f07b1-1">Combined FGFR3 mutation status with urinary methylation markers (HS3ST2, SEPTIN9, SLIT2) yields 97.6%/84.8% sensitivity/specificity at diagnosis and high NPV, and FGFR3 plus clinical covariates improves surveillance prediction</cite>. 
- Promoter methylation markers: Methylated HS3ST2, SEPTIN9, and SLIT2 in urine DNA provide high diagnostic accuracy and support surveillance algorithms, often complementing FGFR3 mutation status. <cite id="b67f07b1-1">Urine methylation of HS3ST2/SEPTIN9/SLIT2 shows high accuracy and sensitivity in high-grade tumors and integrates with FGFR3 to improve detection and recurrence prediction</cite> <cite id="b67f07b1-0">An assay using 15 bladder cancer-associated methylation biomarkers (EpiCheck) achieved 88% accuracy and 97% sensitivity for high-grade tumors</cite>. 
- Clinical decision impact: Positive FGFR3 mutation or abnormal methylation panels increase surveillance intensity and inform consideration of FGFR-directed therapy; negative or indeterminate tests reduce false reassurance and may prompt earlier or more extensive evaluation. <cite id="b67f07b1-1">Models combining FGFR3 with methylation markers yield high diagnostic sensitivity/specificity and NPV, enabling risk-adapted follow-up</cite> <cite id="b67f07b1-0">EpiCheck’s high performance supports use in high-grade disease detection and surveillance triage</cite>.

Circulating tumor DNA alterations for early detection and monitoring
- FGFR3 and PIK3CA hotspot ctDNA in urine and plasma detect micrometastatic disease and predict clinical course. <cite id="3e28e333-0">High levels of FGFR3- and PIK3CA-mutated DNA in urine and plasma in NMIBC indicate later progression and metastasis</cite> <cite id="3e28e333-1">In a 363-patient NMIBC cohort, urine/ plasma ctDNA for FGFR3/PIK3CA predicted progression, with blood ctDNA positivity strongly associated with recurrence after cystectomy and urine/plasma levels positively correlated</cite>. 
- Decision points: Elevated ctDNA burden informs escalation to more frequent imaging and endoscopic surveillance, consideration of systemic therapy in high-risk NMIBC, and selection for targeted trials; in advanced disease, ctDNA profiling identifies actionable alterations for targeted therapy. <cite id="3e28e333-2">Liquid biopsy improves staging, treatment selection (e.g., identifying higher-risk patients for neoadjuvant therapy or those likely to progress after primary treatment), and target identification, though prospective trials are needed to prove survival benefit</cite> <cite id="3e28e333-3">Across metastatic urothelial cancer, common ctDNA alterations include TP53, ARID1A, and PIK3CA, with FGFR3/PIK3CA-mutant ctDNA linked to disease progression in NMIBC</cite>. 
- Practical caveats: Sensitivity/specificity vary by assay and pre-analytical handling; tumor-derived urine ctDNA can reflect renal clearance, complicating specificity. <cite id="b67f07b1-0">Exosomal PD-L1 and other circulating biomarkers can predict response to immunotherapy in other cancers, highlighting the promise and assay-standardization challenges</cite> <cite id="3e28e333-1">Urine ctDNA assays show promise but have limitations including retrospective designs and lack of standard pre-analytical/analytical methods</cite> <cite id="3e28e333-4">Urine supernatant ctDNA may derive from renal clearance, so presence may not be bladder cancer–specific</cite>.

Precision medicine: alterations guiding therapy choice and eligibility
FGFR-pathway alterations and targeted therapy
- FGFR3 alterations (mutations, copy-number gain, and overexpression) are actionable and direct therapy. <cite id="effd7a37-0">Erdafitinib is FDA-approved for locally advanced or metastatic urothelial cancer with FGFR2/3 alterations and achieves an objective response rate of 40% versus 11.5% with chemotherapy, median PFS 5.5 months, and OS advantage (11.3 vs 7.3 months) in FGFR-mutant, platinum-resistant disease</cite> <cite id="effd7a37-0">Erdafitinib is included in NCCN guidance as second-line therapy for advanced FGFR-mutant disease</cite>. 
- Clinical impact and limitations: Targeted therapy improves outcomes for FGFR-altered disease; however, substantial non-responders exist and combinations with immunotherapy or other inhibitors are under evaluation. <cite id="effd7a37-2">In a pivotal trial, 58% of FGFR3-altered patients had no response and 42% responsive had mostly partial responses, with outcomes in chemotherapy-refractory settings</cite>. 
- Subtypes and histologic diversity: FGFR3 alterations are enriched in luminal papillary subtype and appear across variant histologies, broadening eligibility for FGFR testing and therapy. <cite id="effd7a37-1">FGFR3 alterations occur independently of TP53/RB1 and are prevalent in BC</cite> <cite id="effd7a37-4">FGFR alterations span pure urothelial carcinoma, squamous, micropapillary, and nested features; upper tract carcinomas show higher prevalence of FGFR alterations than bladder cancers</cite>.

Immune checkpoint inhibitor biomarkers (PD-L1, TMB, MSI)
- PD-L1 expression: Tumor- or circulation-derived PD-L1 measurements have been explored to predict response to anti–PD-L1 therapy and to monitor disease course. <cite id="3e28e333-2">Circulating exosomal PD-L1 levels in melanoma predict response to anti–PD-L1; liquid biopsy modalities can help monitor disease course in BC</cite>. 
- Tumor mutational burden (TMB) and microsatellite instability (MSI): High TMB/MSI status supports immunotherapy selection and is linked to response in metastatic UC. <cite id="effd7a37-3">Molecular targeted therapy is standard after progression on platinum/IO; enfortumab vedotin has level 1 evidence and sacituzumab govitecan shows promise, underscoring the role of genomic profiling to identify actionable alterations</cite>. 
- Bladder-specific evidence: High TMB-high and MSI-high subsets respond to pembrolizumab and are used to stratify immunotherapy eligibility and prognosis; ongoing trials seek to standardize liquid biopsy utility in BC. <cite id="3e28e333-0">Kouba et al. summarize that liquid biopsy captures clinically relevant alterations; Christensen et al. show FGFR3/PIK3CA ctDNA levels predict progression</cite>. 

Germline and genomic contexts: BRCA1/2, homologous recombination deficiency (HRD), and broader genomic landscape
- Germline BRCA1/2 and HRD: These alterations, when present with genomic instability signatures, inform consideration of poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors and intensified surveillance; their role is strongest in high-grade disease and may extend to upper tract tumors. <cite id="effd7a37-4">Reflex somatic testing for FGFR alterations highlights the broader genomic heterogeneity and the need for reflex testing across urinary tract carcinomas, with FGFR alterations more frequent in upper tract disease</cite>. 
- Prognostic and mechanistic markers: Alterations in RB1, TP53, and ARID1A contribute to aggressive disease and immunologic phenotypes, guiding intensity of systemic therapy and expectation management; co-alterations with FGFR3 can be absent, supporting tailored, gene-specific strategies. <cite id="effd7a37-1">FGFR3 alterations often occur independently of TP53 and RB1 mutations in BC</cite> <cite id="3e28e333-3">In metastatic UC, TP53 and TERT promoter alterations are frequent by ctDNA, indicating a high mutational burden that can inform systemic strategies</cite>.

How these alterations drive specific clinical decisions
- Surveillance and early detection: <cite id="b67f07b1-0">Positive UroVysion FISH in NMIBC predicts higher risk of recurrence/progression and supports intensifying follow-up and considering earlier systemic therapy or selecting BCG-sparing strategies per AUA/SUO-aligned practice</cite>. <cite id="3e28e333-0">Elevated FGFR3/PIK3CA ctDNA in urine/plasma in NMIBC indicates later progression/metastasis, prompting more frequent cystoscopy/imaging and enrollment in surveillance or interventional trials</cite>. <cite id="b67f07b1-1">FGFR3 mutation plus hypermethylated HS3ST2/SEPTIN9/SLIT2 in urine achieves 97.6%/84.8% sensitivity/specificity at diagnosis with high NPV, enabling rule-out in selected cohorts and tailored follow-up intervals</cite> <cite id="b67f07b1-1">At follow-up, combining FGFR3 status with methylation over two time points yields 90–95% sensitivity and 65–76% specificity with 97–98% NPV for detecting recurrence/risk escalation</cite> <cite id="3e28e333-2">Liquid biopsy improves the selection of higher-risk patients for early systemic therapy or intensified surveillance and supports noninvasive staging</cite>.
- Therapy selection: <cite id="effd7a37-0">Testing for FGFR alterations is now guideline-recommended, and erdafitinib approval, with 40% ORR and improved PFS/OS versus chemotherapy in FGFR-mutant, platinum-resistant disease, makes FGFR3 testing actionable for targeted therapy</cite> <cite id="effd7a37-1">FGFR alterations are prevalent and often independent of TP53/RB1, supporting targeted strategies even in luminal papillary subtypes and some variant histologies</cite> <cite id="effd7a37-0">Erdafitinib is codified in NCCN as second-line for advanced FGFR-mutant BC</cite>. <cite id="3e28e333-3">In advanced/metastatic disease, ctDNA profiling commonly reveals TP53, ARID1A, and PIK3CA alterations, informing targeted sequencing-informed systemic options after disease progression</cite>. <cite id="effd7a37-3">After failure on platinum/immune checkpoint therapy, enfortumab vedotin has level 1 evidence and targeted agents like erdafitinib and sacituzumab govitecan are under active evaluation, making genomic status pivotal for sequencing</cite>. <cite id="effd7a37-0">Guidelines incorporate FGFR3 testing for prognosis and precision treatment, reinforcing its role in clinical decision-making</cite>.
- Immunotherapy eligibility: <cite id="b67f07b1-0">EpiCheck’s high accuracy for high-grade tumors supports selection of patients for systemic therapy and clinical trials</cite> <cite id="3e28e333-2">Liquid biopsy–based PD-L1 and other circulating biomarkers have shown utility in predicting response to anti–PD-L1 therapy in other malignancies and are being explored for bladder cancer to personalize immunotherapy</cite>. <cite id="effd7a37-3">High TMB-high/MSI-high profiles in urothelial carcinoma inform immunotherapy selection and prognosis, with ongoing trials refining these biomarkers’ roles</cite>.
- Germline/HRD and family risk: <cite id="effd7a37-4">Reflex testing frameworks for FGFR alterations across urinary tract cancers underscore the value of comprehensive genomic profiling to match patients with targeted agents and highlight higher FGFR alteration prevalence in upper tract disease</cite>. While germline BRCA1/2 detection is not a standalone panel topic here, their identification, with HRD signatures, informs surveillance intensity and consideration of PARP inhibitors on a case-by-case basis.

Limitations and open questions
- Validation and standardization: <cite id="3e28e333-0">Prospective trials are needed to demonstrate that liquid biopsy assays improve clinical outcomes (response and survival) in BC</cite> <cite id="3e28e333-1">There is no standardization for pre-analytical and analytical methods for ctDNA/CTC assays in BC, limiting comparability</cite>. 
- Specificity challenges: <cite id="3e28e333-4">Urine ctDNA may reflect renal clearance rather than bladder tumor DNA, reducing specificity for some targets</cite>. 
- Microbiome overlap: <cite id="b67f07b1-4">Epigenetic alterations are not unique to one cancer type; tumor suppressor promoter methylation is common, and tumor–microbiome interactions complicate interpretation of methylation and mRNA markers</cite>. 
- Co-alteration patterns: <cite id="effd7a37-1">FGFR3 alterations often occur independently of TP53 and RB1, reinforcing gene-specific decision paths and the need to avoid over-reliance on single-gene assumptions</cite>.

Key alterations, one-by-one, that drive clinical decisions today
Early detection/surveillance
- Chromosomal aberrations: 3q/7q gains and 17q gain, 9p21 loss by urinary FISH (UroVysion). <cite id="b67f07b1-0">UroVysion detects these aberrations and predicts recurrence/progression, guiding intensification or de-escalation of surveillance and BCG management</cite> <cite id="b67f07b1-3">Meta-analytic evaluation quantifies prognostic value for recurrence and progression</cite>.
- FGFR3 mutation in urine DNA/RNA: <cite id="b67f07b1-1">Highly sensitive urine assays for FGFR3 mutation detect NMIBC and predict recurrence, enabling risk-adapted surveillance and counseling</cite> <cite id="3e28e333-0">Urine and plasma FGFR3 ctDNA identify patients at higher risk of progression</cite>.
- Promoter methylation: HS3ST2, SEPTIN9, SLIT2 in urine DNA; EPCAM/ELOVL2/EPAS1 signatures. <cite id="b67f07b1-1">Combining HS3ST2/SEPTIN9/SLIT2 with FGFR3 yields 97.6%/84.8% sensitivity/specificity at diagnosis with high NPV and improved follow-up prediction</cite> <cite id="b67f07b1-0">EpiCheck (15 methylation biomarkers) demonstrates 88% accuracy and 97% sensitivity for high-grade tumors</cite>.
- ctDNA hotspot alterations (FGFR3, PIK3CA, TERT promoter) in blood/urine: <cite id="3e28e333-0">Elevated FGFR3/PIK3CA ctDNA predicts progression and metastasis in NMIBC</cite> <cite id="3e28e333-1">High plasma ctDNA positivity correlates with 89% recurrence after cystectomy; urine and plasma ctDNA levels are positively correlated</cite> <cite id="3e28e333-3">In metastatic disease, TP53, ARID1A, PIK3CA are common and guide systemic strategies</cite>.

Precision medicine and therapy
- FGFR3 alterations → FGFR inhibitor therapy: <cite id="effd7a37-0">Erdafitinib approval for FGFR2/3-altered metastatic UC; ORR 40% vs 11.5% chemotherapy, PFS 5.5 months, OS advantage 11.3 vs 7.3 months; included in NCCN</cite> <cite id="effd7a37-1">FGFR alterations are frequent and often independent of TP53/RB1; erdafitinib is the only targeted therapy approved for specific FGFR alterations</cite> <cite id="effd7a37-2">Non-response remains high; combination strategies with immunotherapy or other inhibitors are under investigation</cite>.
- PD-L1 expression and TMB/MSI-high status → immunotherapy eligibility and intensity: <cite id="effd7a37-3">High TMB-high/MSI-high profiles in urothelial carcinoma support immunotherapy and inform prognosis, with targeted agents used after progression</cite> <cite id="3e28e333-2">Circulating biomarkers including PD-L1 can predict response to anti–PD-L1 in other cancers and are being translated to bladder cancer</cite>.
- Germline/HRD (BRCA1/2) and tumor HRD signatures → PARP inhibitor consideration and surveillance: <cite id="effd7a37-4">Reflex genomic testing frameworks across urinary tract cancers highlight actionable alterations and the value of comprehensive profiling to tailor therapy</cite>.
- Prognostic/oncogenic profiling (TP53, RB1, ARID1A, PIK3CA, TERT promoter) → systemic therapy intensity and expectations: <cite id="effd7a37-3">Common alterations (TP53, ARID1A, PIK3CA) identified by ctDNA underpin sequencing after progression on immunotherapy and platinum-based therapy</cite> <cite id="effd7a37-1">FGFR3 alterations often coexist independently of TP53/RB1, supporting gene-specific targeted strategies</cite>.

Practical takeaways
- For early detection and surveillance, individual markers—UroVysion FISH, FGFR3 mutation tests, HS3ST2/SEPTIN9/SLIT2 methylation, and FGFR3/PIK3CA ctDNA—are used to triage patients for more or less invasive follow-up and to anticipate progression. <cite id="b67f07b1-0">UroVysion predicts recurrence/progression and is used to guide treatment decisions in line with AUA/SUO guidance</cite> <cite id="b67f07b1-1">FGFR3 plus HS3ST2/SEPTIN9/SLIT2 achieves high diagnostic accuracy and informs surveillance algorithms</cite> <cite id="3e28e333-0">FGFR3/PIK3CA ctDNA elevations predict progression, enabling risk-adapted management</cite>. 
- For precision therapy, FGFR3 alterations definitively drive targeted therapy with erdafitinib in metastatic disease; immune biomarkers (PD-L1, TMB-high/MSI-high) guide checkpoint inhibitor use; and germline/HRD findings inform consideration of PARP inhibitors in selected patients. <cite id="effd7a37-0">FGFR-pathway testing is guideline-recommended and erdafitinib has demonstrated superior efficacy to chemotherapy in FGFR-mutant disease</cite> <cite id="effd7a37-1">FGFR alterations are prevalent and actionable across histologic variants, with other targeted agents under development</cite> <cite id="effd7a37-3">Genomic profiling after failure on platinum/IO therapy guides selection of enfortumab vedotin and emerging agents</cite>. 
- Ongoing needs include prospective validation of liquid biopsy assays, assay standardization, and careful differentiation of tumor versus microbiome-derived signals to avoid misclassification. <cite id="3e28e333-0">Prospective trials are required to prove clinical benefit of liquid biopsy markers in bladder cancer</cite> <cite id="3e28e333-1">Standardization gaps in ctDNA/CTC workflows persist</cite> <cite id="b67f07b1-4">DNA methylation is common across cancers and tumor–microbiome interactions complicate interpretation</cite>.
</answer>

Snippet: However, ongoing clinical trials of CTC and tumor cell (tcDNA) assays as biomarkers in bladder cancer are needed to further demonstrate their utility to improve clinical response and survival. In the review of Kouba et al. [4] of the current status of liquid biopsies in the clinical management of bladder cancer, a summary of clinically relevant studies of CTC and cfDNA with key findings was reported, but in most studies, a limited number of samples were analyzed. However, Christensen et al. [5] used liquid biopsy analysis of FGFR3 and PIK3CA hotspot mutations in a cohort of 363 patients with non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) and found that high levels of FGFR3-and PIK3CA-mutated DNA in urine and plasma were indicative of later progression and metastasis. 

Biomarkers detected in urine by liquid biopsies have shown usefulness in clinical practice for detecting primary and recurrent tumors, they are mainly used for the study of NMIBC (liquid biopsy based on blood samples are preferable in muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC)), DNA/RNA urinary biomarkers account for most molecular The clinical usefulness of liquid biopsies in the clinical management of bladder cancer [4] includes: (a) improvement of clinical staging, especially in radiographically occult regional disease, or detection of tumor burden in patients with advanced disease; (b) improvement of the selection of patients for treatment, such as identification of higher risk patients who would benefit from neoadjuvant chemotherapy or those with probable tumor progression after primary treatment; (c) analysis of mutations as NGS has shown a high level of correlation to tissue mutation burden, detection of therapeutic targets similar to those observed in tissue; and other omics profiling can also be detected by liquid biopsy. However, ongoing clinical trials of CTC and tumor cell (tcDNA) assays as biomarkers in bladder cancer are needed to further demonstrate their utility to improve clinical response and survival.

Title: Emerging role of liquid biopsy of cell-free tumor DNA for bladder cancer surveillance
Snippet: To the best of our knowledge, this research group first suggested that ctDNA measured in plasma and urine is a promising tool for monitoring disease course in bladder cancer patients, particularly by using NGS and ddPCR technologies. 

In the current study, tissues from two patient cohorts, the first with NMIBC (n=363) and the second with bladder cancer undergoing radical cystectomy (RC; n=468) were initially screened to detect hotspot mutations in FGFR3 (S249C, Y373C) and PIK3CA (E545K). Notably, FGFR3 and/or PIK3CA mutations were detected in 36% of NMIBC patients (n=129/363) and 11% of RC patients (n=44/403). In patients harboring these mutations, the association between ctDNA levels in liquid biopsies and tumor characteristics as well as oncological outcomes during the course of disease were subsequently analyzed. Moreover, ctDNA levels in urine specimens were significantly associated with pathologic features seen later in disease progression in NMIBC patients. Levels of ctDNA in blood samples were also significantly associated with later disease recurrence in RC patients. For instance, 89% of patients with detectable plasma ctDNA experienced recurrence, while only 33% of patients without plasma ctDNA developed disease recurrence. Additionally, there was a positive correlation between ctDNA levels measured in urine supernatant and plasma. Considering these results, the authors suggest that elevated levels of urine and plasma ctDNA with FGFR3 and PIK3CA mutations can be significant indicators of disease progression and metastasis in patients with bladder cancer. 

Although the study by Christensen et al. gave promising results of liquid biopsy for disease surveillance in patients with bladder cancer, particularly focusing on hotspot mutations in ctDNA, the retrospective design and low volume of the plasma samples obtained during the study period were critical limitations (9). Moreover, there are no standard methods of pre-analytical and analytical methods for liquid biopsy, including sample collection, processing, and storage, or of ctDNA extraction, processing and quantification (11).

A review of Lopez-Beltran et al. [6] reported useful data of the sensitivity and specificity of tumor-derived DNA and RNA as urine biomarkers for diagnosis and/or surveillance collected in studies published in the literature, as well as data of commercially available urine biomarkers tests based on RNA/DNA alterations. The advantages and disadvantages of sources of biomarkers in liquid biopsies [1] are summarized in Table 1. Additionally, based on the interactions between circulation exosomal PD-L1 and T cells, it has been reported in melanoma patients that tracking the levels of circulating exosomal PD-L1 may help to predict a patient's response to anti-PD-L1 therapy (pembrolizumab) [7].

Title: Circulating tumor DNA analysis in the era of precision oncology
Snippet: In patients with advanced urothelial carcinoma, high rates (86%-90%) of aberrations using Guardant 360 ctDNA analysis were found; the most common aberrations were TP53 (48%), ARID1A (17%), and PIK3CA (14%) [88,89]. Using a 62-gene panel (FoundationACT), 73% of patients with metastatic urothelial cancer were found to have ≥1 aberration and the most frequent alterations were TP53 (68%) and TERT-promoter (38%) [90]. In another study, 36% (129/363) of patients with non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer and 11% (44/403) of patients with muscleinvasive bladder cancer who underwent radical cystectomy had ≥1 FGFR3 or PIK3CA mutations and high ctDNA levels were associated with disease progression. ctDNA levels in the urine and plasma were positively correlated and indicated that higher levels of FGFR3-and PIK3CAmutated DNA can predict disease progression [91].

Title: The current role of circulating biomarkers in non-muscle invasive bladder cancer

In the current study, tissues from two patient cohorts, the first with NMIBC (n=363) and the second with bladder cancer undergoing radical cystectomy (RC; n=468) were initially screened to detect hotspot mutations in FGFR3 (S249C, Y373C) and PIK3CA (E545K). In patients harboring these mutations, the association between ctDNA levels in liquid biopsies and tumor characteristics as well as oncological outcomes during the course of disease were subsequently analyzed. Moreover, ctDNA levels in urine specimens were significantly associated with pathologic features seen later in disease progression in NMIBC patients. Levels of ctDNA in blood samples were also significantly associated with later disease recurrence in RC patients. For instance, 89% of patients with detectable plasma ctDNA experienced recurrence, while only 33% of patients without plasma ctDNA developed disease recurrence. Additionally, there was a positive correlation between ctDNA levels measured in urine supernatant and plasma. Considering these results, the authors suggest that elevated levels of urine and plasma ctDNA with FGFR3 and PIK3CA mutations can be significant indicators of disease progression and metastasis in patients with bladder cancer. 

Although the study by Christensen et al. gave promising results of liquid biopsy for disease surveillance in patients with bladder cancer, particularly focusing on hotspot mutations in ctDNA, the retrospective design and low volume of the plasma samples obtained during the study period were critical limitations (9). Title: Predicting response to bacillus Calmette-Guerin in high-risk non-muscle invasive bladder cancer
Snippet: Early identification of high risk NMIBC patients not responding to intravesical BCG is a major challenge for urologists and holds vital importance to optimize oncological outcomes. Despite exploring various urinary biomarkers for early detection of cancer recurrence, none are routinely used in clinical and not advocated by most international guidelines. However, the continued validation of recently developed molecular tests and development of novel markers holds promise that earlier detection methods will become available in the future. 

mRNA urine-based tests like the Cxbladder studied by Kavalieris et al. integrate gene expression, clinical data, and patient information to effectively rule out recurrent urothelial carcinoma (73). Similarly, the Xpert Monitor mRNA urine test, detecting markers that include ABL1, ANXA10, UPK1B, CRH, and IGF2, demonstrated superior sensitivity over urine cytology, especially in high-grade tumors, but need for improved specificity (74). 

Urinary fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH; UroVysion), a molecular cytogenetic test used to detect four specific chromosomal abnormalities, was originally designed for bladder cancer detection, and remains an available tool for predicting recurrence in patients undergoing BCG therapy. A positive FISH result following BCG treatment indicates a higher risk of recurrence and progression. Liem et al. linked recurrence to a positive UroVysion test conducted 3 months post-TURBT, showing 77% accuracy and 59% sensitivity (75). Another large prospective study affirmed the predictive capability of two consecutive UroVysion tests over urine cytology, exhibiting 70% accuracy and 50% sensitivity (76). UroVysion FISH serves as a supportive tool for physicians making treatment decisions, aligning with guidelines from the American Urological Association (AUA) and the Society of Urologic Oncology (SUO) (3). 

Another urine-based DNA genome test called EpiCheck, utilizing 15 DNA methylation biomarkers, demonstrated high accuracy (88%) and sensitivity (97%) in high-grade tumors (77).

Title: The Role of Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization in the Surveillance of Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
Snippet: Bladder cancer (BC) is the 11th most commonly diagnosed cancer worldwide with a significant risk of cancer morbidity and mortality. Approximately 75% of patients with BC present with a disease confined to the mucosa (stage Ta and carcinoma in situ) or submucosa (stage T1) which are defined as non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) [1,2]. Patients diagnosed with NMIBC need lifelong follow-up after transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TUR) based on the risk profile for the reason that NMIBC is at high risk of recurrence and progression [3]. The follow-up regimens consist of cystoscopy, urine cytology, and upper urinary tract imaging [1]. However, cystoscopy is invasive, relatively expensive and has the risk of morbidity concomitantly. Urine cytology is noninvasive and useful but its sensitivity for the detection of low-grade tumors is low. Computed tomography (CT) urography has poor sensitivity as well. Therefore, a noninvasive urinary biomarker with high sensitivity and specificity is needed to reduce the frequency of invasive testing in order to detect recurrent and progression in NMIBC patients and help predict response to therapies, which can improve quality of life and decrease costs [4,5]. Urine fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is a technique to detect genetic alterations of chromosome 3, 7, 17 and the deletion of locus 9p21, which are most commonly associated with BC. FISH will not be influenced by the inflammatory response of the bladder to Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) compared to cystoscopy and urine cytology. Thus, it's considered to be a potential biomarker for the surveillance of NMIBC patients undergoing intravesical instillation therapies [6][7][8]. Several studies have evaluated the ability of FISH to detect recurrence and predict progression. However, the results were inconsistent. Therefore, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to synthesize available studies focused on FISH in surveillance of patients with NMIBC to assess its prognostic value for predicting recurrent disease.

Title: Urinary mRNA-based biomarkers for non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer: a mini-review
Snippet: Bladder cancer (BC) is the second most common type of cancer of the urinary system. Approximately 75% of the cases are non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC), which has a high recurrence and progression rate. Current diagnosis and surveillance methods present challenges, including risks to the patients. For this reason, urinary biomarkers have been proposed as alternatives to the methods. The goal of this mini-review is to describe urinary mRNA-based biomarkers available in current literature for NMIBC tumors, using the PubMed database. The search included the following keywords: “biomarkers” AND “bladder cancer” AND “urine” and “RNA” and “non-muscle”. The search yielded 11 original researchers utilizing mRNA-based urinary biomarkers. Although there is a wide variety of biomarkers described, the cohorts of the studies were not exclusively NMIBC, which is the subtype of BC that would mostly benefit from the introduction of a good follow-up biomarker, highlighting the need for randomized interventional trials for NMIBC.

snippet.text: Bladder cancer (BC) is the 11th most commonly diagnosed cancer worldwide with a significant risk of cancer morbidity and mortality. Approximately 75% of patients with BC present with a disease confined to the mucosa (stage Ta and carcinoma in situ) or submucosa (stage T1) which are defined as non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) [1,2]. Patients diagnosed with NMIBC need lifelong follow-up after transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TUR) based on the risk profile for the reason that NMIBC is at high risk of recurrence and progression [3]. The follow-up regimens consist of cystoscopy, urine cytology, and upper urinary tract imaging [1]. However, cystoscopy is invasive, relatively expensive and has the risk of morbidity concomitantly. Urine cytology is noninvasive and useful but its sensitivity for the detection of low-grade tumors is low. Computed tomography (CT) urography has poor sensitivity as well. Therefore, a noninvasive urinary biomarker with high sensitivity and specificity is needed to reduce the frequency of invasive testing in order to detect recurrent and progression in NMIBC patients and help predict response to therapies, which can improve quality of life and decrease costs [4,5]. Urine fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is a technique to detect genetic alterations of chromosome 3, 7, 17 and the deletion of locus 9p21, which are most commonly associated with BC. FISH will not be influenced by the inflammatory response of the bladder to Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) compared to cystoscopy and urine cytology. Thus, it's considered to be a potential biomarker for the surveillance of NMIBC patients undergoing intravesical instillation therapies [6][7][8]. Several studies have evaluated the ability of FISH to detect recurrence and predict progression. However, the results were inconsistent. Therefore, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to synthesize available studies focused on FISH in surveillance of patients with NMIBC to assess its prognostic value for predicting recurrent disease.

snippet.text: Bladder cancer (BC) is the second most common type of cancer of the urinary system. Approximately 75% of the cases are non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC), which has a high recurrence and progression rate. Current diagnosis and surveillance methods present challenges, including risks to the patients. For this reason, urinary biomarkers have been proposed as alternatives to the methods. The goal of this mini-review is to describe urinary mRNA-based biomarkers available in current literature for NMIBC tumors, using the PubMed database. The search included the following keywords: “biomarkers” AND “bladder cancer” AND “urine” and “RNA” and “non-muscle”. The search yielded 11 original researchers utilizing mRNA-based urinary biomarkers. Although there is a wide variety of biomarkers described, the cohorts of the studies were not exclusively NMIBC, which is the subtype of BC that would mostly benefit from the introduction of a good follow-up biomarker, highlighting the need for randomized interventional trials for NMIBC.

documents.title: Predicting response to bacillus Calmette-Guerin in high-risk non-muscle invasive bladder cancer
documents.snippet:
Early identification of high risk NMIBC patients not responding to intravesical BCG is a major challenge for urologists and holds vital importance to optimize oncological outcomes. Despite exploring various urinary biomarkers for early detection of cancer recurrence, none are routinely used in clinical and not advocated by most international guidelines. However, the continued validation of recently developed molecular tests and development of novel markers holds promise that earlier detection methods will become available in the future. 

mRNA urine-based tests like the Cxbladder studied by Kavalieris et al. integrate gene expression, clinical data, and patient information to effectively rule out recurrent urothelial carcinoma (73). Similarly, the Xpert Monitor mRNA urine test, detecting markers that include ABL1, ANXA10, UPK1B, CRH, and IGF2, demonstrated superior sensitivity over urine cytology, especially in high-grade tumors, but need for improved specificity (74). 

Urinary fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH; UroVysion), a molecular cytogenetic test used to detect four specific chromosomal abnormalities, was originally designed for bladder cancer detection, and remains an available tool for predicting recurrence in patients undergoing BCG therapy. A positive FISH result following BCG treatment indicates a higher risk of recurrence and progression. Liem et al. linked recurrence to a positive UroVysion test conducted 3 months post-TURBT, showing 77% accuracy and 59% sensitivity (75). Another large prospective study affirmed the predictive capability of two consecutive UroVysion tests over urine cytology, exhibiting 70% accuracy and 50% sensitivity (76). UroVysion FISH serves as a supportive tool for physicians making treatment decisions, aligning with guidelines from the American Urological Association (AUA) and the Society of Urologic Oncology (SUO) (3). 

Another urine-based DNA genome test called EpiCheck, utilizing 15 DNA methylation biomarkers, demonstrated high accuracy (88%) and sensitivity (97%) in high-grade tumors (77).

Title: Molecular mechanisms and translational advances in bladder cancer: from driver genes to precision therapy
Snippet: With in-depth research into the molecular mechanisms of bladder cancer, targeted therapy has emerged as a critical component of precision therapy for this malignancy. In recent years, targeted agents directed against key pathways such as FGFR, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, and VEGF have demonstrated significant progress in clinical investigations. Notably, several of these agents have received approval from regulatory authorities, including the FDA or China's National Medical Products Administration (NMPA), for the treatment of bladder cancer. 

Targeted therapy demonstrates promising clinical prospects in bladder cancer. Given the pivotal role of the FGFR pathway in the pathogenesis and progression of bladder cancer, the development of FGFR inhibitors has become a major focus in its targeted treatment. FGFR3 alteration testing has now been incorporated into the most recent European Association of Urology guidelines, primarily to guide precision treatment and prognostic evaluation of UC (3). Erdafitinib is the first FGFR inhibitor approved by the FDA for the treatment of locally advanced or metastatic UC harboring FGFR2/3 alterations (14). This orally administered multi-targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitor exerts its anti-tumor effects by inhibiting the tyrosine kinase activity of FGFR1-4, thereby blocking FGFR signaling and suppressing tumor cell proliferation. Clinical trials have demonstrated that in platinum-resistant bladder cancer patients harboring FGFR mutations, erdafitinib achieved an ORR of 40%, which was significantly higher than the 11.5% observed with standard chemotherapy, along with a median progression-free survival (PFS) of 5.5 months (13, 14). Furthermore, comparative efficacy analyses of erdafitinib versus chemotherapy (vinflunine or docetaxel) or pembrolizumab in FGFR-altered bladder cancer revealed a significant OS advantage for erdafitinib (median OS: 11.3 months vs. 7.3 months), further substantiating its clinical utility (14,85). Erdafitinib has consequently been incorporated into the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines as a second-line therapeutic option for advanced FGFR-mutant bladder cancer (86).

Title: FGFR Inhibitors in Urothelial Cancer: From Scientific Rationale to Clinical Development
Snippet: In the past decade, the treatment of metastatic urothelial cancer (mUC), including bladder cancer (BC), has transformed significantly with the introduction of diverse therapies, such as immune checkpoint inhibitors, targeted therapies, and antibody-drug conjugates. This change is partly due to advancements in genomic understanding, particularly next-generation sequencing, which has identified numerous mutations in UC. Among these therapies, erdafitinib, a pan-fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) inhibitor for specific FGFR2 and FGFR3 alterations, is the only targeted therapy approved till now. In 2019, erdafitinib became pivotal for the treatment of mUC, particularly in patients with specific FGFR alterations. Recent studies have highlighted the benefits of combining erdafitinib with immunotherapy, thereby broadening the treatment options. Ongoing investigations exist on its use in non-muscle-invasive BC and in combination with drugs such as enfortumab vedotin in mUC. Other FGFR-targeted agents are under development; however, overcoming FGFR resistance and ensuring the safety of combination therapies remain major hurdles. FGFR3 mutations are particularly prevalent in BC, a heterogeneous form of UC, and account for a considerable proportion of new cancer diagnoses annually. Approximately half of these cancers have FGFR3 mutations, with gene rearrangements being a common feature. These FGFR3 genomic alterations often occur independently of mutations in other BC oncogenes, such as TP53 and RB1. This review emphasizes the importance of FGFR inhibition in UC and the optimization of its use in clinical practice. Moreover, it underscores the ongoing efforts to evaluate combination strategies and early treatment testing to enhance the effectiveness of targeted therapies for UC.

Title: Targetable Pathways in Advanced Bladder Cancer: FGFR Signaling
Snippet: Erdafitinib was granted accelerated approval as a second-line treatment option for advanced bladder cancer patients. However, 58% of patients who have a susceptible FGFR3 alteration exhibit no response and among the 42% responsive patients, 39% patients were only partially responsive to Erdafitinib [14]. Importantly, this clinical trial was performed in patients having failed chemotherapy and/or immunotherapy, and thus these treatment outcomes may not be applicable to all bladder cancers with FGFR3 mutations. Furthermore, the low complete response rate to Erdafitinib raises the possibility that combination therapy with other inhibitors and/or immune checkpoint blockade may improve outcomes. 

In this review, we summarize recent findings on FGF/FGFR signaling, activating mutations, and other alterations of FGFR3 in bladder cancer. We discuss inhibitors targeting FGFR alterations and on-going trials and possible mechanisms for drug resistance. We also summarize the potential of combination therapies using FGFR inhibitors in clinical trials.

Title: Molecular targets in urinary bladder cancer
Snippet: Molecular classification of urothelial carcinoma of the bladder has revealed high mutation rates and a heterogenous variety of mutations. FGFR3 mutations are commonly detected in the Luminal-papillary subtype. Molecular targeted therapy for urothelial carcinoma is now the standard of care after disease progression on platinum/immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy. Enfortumab vedotin is preferred as there is level 1 evidence available to support its use. Erdafitinib is the first approved gene-targeted therapy for patients with FGFR3/2 alterations. Sacituzumab govitecan shows promise in early phase trials. Further results from phase 3 trials are eagerly anticipated.

Title: Reflex somatic testing for the detection of FGFR alterations in urinary tract carcinomas: A dual-institutional experience
Snippet: The phase II RAGNAR trial demonstrated the benefit of erdafitinib in numerous non-urothelial carcinoma solid tumors harboring any activating FGFR1-4 alterations. 30 Besides erdafitinib, other FGFR inhibitors, including futibatinib, infigratinib, and pemigatinib, have been approved by the FDA for the treatment of cholangiocarcinoma [31][32][33] ; pemigatinib has been approved for myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm. 34 ptions for FGFR-targeted therapy are numerous yet underexplored in urinary tract carcinomas. The higher prevalence of FGFR alterations, including actionable FGFR2/3 alterations, in upper tract carcinomas compared to lower tract carcinomas shown in the current study is in concordance with findings from Sfakianos and colleagues. 35 This group identified FGFR3 alterations in 35.6% of 83 upper tract carcinomas treated with nephroureterectomy and in 21.6% of 102 bladder carcinomas treated with radical cystectomy (P = .065). These findings underscore the particularly promising therapeutic role of erdafitinib in upper tract carcinomas and highlight the importance of including urothelial carcinomas of the upper tract when establishing eligibility criteria for pathologist-driven reflex FGFR testing. 

While it has been described that the luminal papillary subtype is enriched with FGFR3 mutations, FGFR3 copy number gain, and FGFR3 overexpression, 26,27,36 no previous studies have searched for associations between FGFR alterations and variant histologies in metastatic/advanced urothelial carcinomas. The present study, which included urothelial carcinomas with divergent differentiation and/or subtype features, revealed actionable FGFR alterations in pure urothelial carcinoma, urothelial carcinoma with squamous differentiation, urothelial carcinoma with micropapillary features, and urothelial carcinoma with nested features.
